Buoyed by robust local demand and improved export performance, the Hong Kong economy maintained steady growth momentum in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The local economic outlook continues to be influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the normalization of monetary policies by major central banks, the stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the short term, although local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate, some upside risks persist.  The Hong Kong economy maintained its growth momentum in the second half of 2017. The seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, comparable to the average growth rate of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Figure 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow robustly and remained one of the main drivers of GDP growth. The robust consumption growth was attributable to favourable employment and income conditions, sustained consumer optimism, and positive wealth effects stemming from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activities weakened, an increase in corporate capital expenditure led to a significant rise in overall investment expenditure in the last quarter after three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance further improved, benefiting from better global trade growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism (Figure 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services made a positive contribution. Figure 3.1 Growth Rate of Real GDP and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components; Figure 3.2 Real Exports and Imports.  Sustained economic growth momentum drove an increase in employment in the second half of 2017. During the period, total employment rose by about 0.7% to over 3.85 million, with the most significant increases occurring in the construction, financial and business services, and public administration, social and personal services sectors. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, there were signs of further improvement in labour productivity. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance is projected to continue benefiting from an improved outlook for global economic growth and a gradual recovery in inbound tourism. Locally, private consumption is expected to continue growing, primarily due to favourable labour market conditions. Given that Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise, Feature 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption. Regarding local gross fixed capital formation, building and construction activities are expected to grow steadily, benefiting from increased housing supply and the ongoing rollout of infrastructure projects. Although an improving economic environment is likely to stimulate corporate capital expenditure, a possible rate hike could exert a negative impact. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2018 to be between 3% and 4%, while growth projections by international institutions and private analysts range from 2% to 4%. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook remains subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in previous chapters, Mainland China's economic performance amid tightening financial conditions, and the trend of local asset markets.  Local inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, though there were signs of a slight pick-up in month-on-month inflation momentum in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the Core Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, comparable to the average increase of about 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the Core Inflation Rate, calculated on a three-month annualized basis to reflect inflation momentum, edged up slightly to 2.8% in January 2018 (Figure 3.3). Prices of both tradable goods and services increased. The recovery in new private residential rents since mid-2016 may have also contributed to inflation momentum to some extent (Figure 3.4). Furthermore, labour cost pressures have remained moderate in recent quarters (Figure 3.5). Figure 3.3 Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation; Figure 3.4 CPI Rental Component and Market Rents; Figure 3.5 Unit Labour Cost and Average Wage per Employee. Given that global inflation remains moderate and local cost increases are stable, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to remain moderate in 2018, although the Core Inflation Rate may gradually recover from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, inflation pressures may increase in the second half of 2018 due to the pass-through effect from growth in new private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation to be a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government's forecast for the Core Inflation Rate is 2.5%. Although the inflation outlook is moderate, upside risks remain. On the external front, unexpected increases in global inflation or commodity prices could boost local inflation momentum. Locally, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly two decades (Figure 3.6). The current output gap is estimated to be close to zero; if the labour market tightens significantly, it could exert additional upside pressure on inflation. Figure 3.6 Unemployment Rate.  Following the 2008 global financial crisis, low interest rates led to an increase in mortgage indebtedness among Hong Kong households. As US dollar interest rates normalize, Hong Kong dollar interest rates will eventually rise in tandem, leading to a corresponding increase in future household mortgage repayment burdens and thus weighing on household consumption. Therefore, this feature examines the impact of increased mortgage repayment burdens on private consumption in Hong Kong. The mortgage repayment burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt servicing payments (i.e., interest payments plus principal amortization) to income. Figure B3.1 illustrates the role of the mortgage repayment burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, and wealth and collateral effects induced by asset price changes mentioned in standard economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage repayment burden, interest rate shocks also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, thereby changing households' disposable income. This effect will be amplified as the outstanding mortgage loan balance increases. Moreover, the principal amortization amount varies with changes in the outstanding mortgage loan balance, which also affects private consumption through changes in household disposable income. Figure B3.1 Determinants of Private Consumption.  To measure the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption, we estimated the Outstanding Mortgage Debt Service Ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike existing mortgage repayment burden indicators that apply only to new mortgage liabilities, the OMDSR covers the total outstanding mortgage liabilities of all households, which is more closely related to total private consumption. We largely adopted the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, employing a standard formula for fixed instalment payments to measure the OMDSR: where Dt is the amount of outstanding residential mortgage loans in the banking sector, Yt is the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st are the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans, respectively. To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage repayment burden of the entire household sector, it is appropriate to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt service ratio indicators. Figure B3.2 shows the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to 2017, as well as the median ratio of mortgage and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on the quinquennial population census. In the early 2000s, both ratios exhibited a downward trend, consistent with the decline in overall household mortgage borrowing following the bursting of the property bubble in 1997 and the concurrent sharp fall in mortgage interest rates. Despite a significant rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, attributable to the macro-prudential measures taken by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. Additionally, the extension of the maturity of new mortgage loans also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments. Figure B3.2 OMDSR and Median Ratio of Mortgage and Loan Repayments to Income.  We also compared the OMDSR with the banks' Debt Servicing Ratio (DSR), which represents the actual debt servicing-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants at banks. As shown in Figure B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than the banks' DSR, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing ones. Since existing mortgages were established when property prices were lower, their corresponding payments are lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, an outstanding mortgage repayment burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e., the OMDSR) will be lower than a burden indicator for new mortgages only (i.e., the banks' DSR). Furthermore, the banks' DSR is higher because banks comply with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements by including non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the DSR. After the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and the banks' DSR remained stable, primarily due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential regulation on mortgage lending, which set a cap on the banks' DSR; this measure also helped stabilize the OMDSR. Figure B3.3 OMDSR and Banks' New Mortgage Debt Servicing Ratio.  Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt service ratio indicators, but it possesses greater timeliness and can reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage liabilities, not just new mortgage liabilities. Therefore, we believe that using the OMDSR allows for an assessment of the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption. To evaluate the impact of the mortgage repayment burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimated an error-correction model following the methodologies of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real private consumption per household on average) and its determinants is represented by an error-correction term in the short-run equation. Based on existing theory and empirical evidence, we selected real income (proxied by household median income deflated by the CPI), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential prices and the Hang Seng Index, respectively, deflated by the CPI), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2017, total loans continued to increase, but the growth rate slowed compared with the first half. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Should global financial market sentiment shift abruptly, fluctuations in capital flows could increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate against the US dollar fluctuated between 7.799 and 7.827 (Figure 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly from September to November 2017 and remained at levels around 7.80. This was mainly due to rising funding demands from new share fundraising activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and year-end, which led to tighter liquidity conditions. Consequently, carry trade activity slowed, and there was an increase in the covering of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. As the tight liquidity conditions eased and demand for US dollars for commercial purposes rose towards year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate weakened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, despite increased volatility in global financial markets (particularly equity markets), the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner. During the reporting period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar weakened, but the weak-side conversion guarantee was not triggered (Figure 4.2). Figure 4.1: Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate; Figure 4.2: Capital Flow Indicators. The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index fluctuated slightly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressure as the US dollar weakened further (Figure 4.3). This is broadly consistent with the trend of the US dollar against most major currencies. Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which has limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index continued to closely track movements in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. Securities investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics show that both local and non-resident equity securities investments recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved regional economic prospects and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Debt securities investment by non-residents also recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting the outflow of debt investment by local residents. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that, due to market optimism regarding economic prospects and corporate earnings, both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017. In recent weeks, survey data showed that despite adjustments in global financial markets, equity investments continued to record inflows, while bond investments recorded slight outflows (Figure 4.4). Figure 4.4: Market Survey on Equity and Bond-Related Capital Flows. Looking ahead, as the US monetary policy normalization process continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will likely widen, potentially leading to increased carry trade activity. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side conversion guarantee being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the Linked Exchange Rate System. Meanwhile, given that the pace of US monetary policy normalization remains unclear and global macro-financial conditions and market sentiment are volatile, fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar capital flows and the exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate under the currency board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve's interest rate hikes and continued balance sheet reduction, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained loose in the second half of 2017 and recently. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased further by 1.4%, primarily driven by the growth in certificates of indebtedness issued for note issuance (Figure 4.5). As the conversion guarantee was not triggered, the total ending balance remained largely unchanged from the total outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, staying at approximately HK$1,226.8 billion. Of this, the total ending balance decreased, while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills (totaling HK$80 billion) to meet banks' substantial liquidity management needs. Entering 2018, despite equity market adjustments, the monetary base remained stable. Figure 4.5: Components of the Monetary Base. Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply continued to grow in the second half of 2017, albeit at a slower pace. The growth rate of the broad Hong Kong dollar money supply (HKD M3) slowed from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits increased slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Figure 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew faster in the second half, partly due to a buoyant asset market and rising investment demand. Analysis of corresponding assets shows that the growth in HKD M3 was supported on one hand by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Figure 4.6), and on the other hand, weighed down by net outflows of Hong Kong dollar funds from the non-bank private sector and a contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets. Figure 4.6: Changes in HKD M3 and Corresponding Assets. On the other hand, growth in foreign currency deposits was mixed. Partly reflecting the depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits declined from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after falling for over two years, rebounded significantly in the second half, rising by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by the recent recovery in Renminbi deposits. Due to the slowdown in the growth of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar deposits, total deposits of authorized institutions increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with a growth rate of 5.6% in the first half. For the full year of 2017, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, roughly similar to 2016. Figure 4.7: Deposit Growth. Between September and December 2017, rising funding demands from new share fundraising activities and banks' cautious approach to liquidity management at month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (Figure 4.8). Compared with six months prior, the overnight and 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (based on monthly averages). The negative interest rate differential between 1-month to 3-month Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interbank offered rates also narrowed correspondingly. Figure 4.8: Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly mirroring the trend of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 63 basis points to close at 1.52% at the end of 2017, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds increased by a smaller margin of 33 basis points to close at 1.83% at the end of 2017 (Figure 4.9). Figure 4.9: Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Mortgage Loan Rate for New Loans. Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demands subsided, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates declined in early January. Thereafter, despite adjustments in global and local equity markets, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates remained broadly stable. The overnight and 3-month HIBOR closed at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at the end of February 2018. At the retail level, although bank lending rates rose in line with the increase in HIBOR, banks' funding costs generally remained low due to the large deposit base. Despite intense competition in the mortgage lending business, the average mortgage loan rate for new loans rose gradually by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Figure 4.9), broadly following the upward trend of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Composite Interest Rate, which measures retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding costs, rose briefly in October due to increased funding demands from new share fundraising activities but remained soft for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at the end of December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalization continues and other major economies may initiate rate normalization, Hong Kong dollar interest rates may face greater upward pressure. Meanwhile, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro-financial conditions may increase volatility in capital flows. However, the substantial Hong Kong dollar monetary base can serve as a buffer to help moderate any overly rapid rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates. Furthermore, banks' prudent liquidity management and the availability of discounting through the discount window also help suppress excessive volatility in interbank offered rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. The loan growth rate was as high as 10.2% in the first half but slowed to 5.3% in the second half (Figure 4.10). In the second half of 2017, growth in loans used in Hong Kong and loans used outside Hong Kong both slowed. Analyzed by currency, due to improving local economic conditions and relatively low Hong Kong dollar funding costs, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, while foreign currency loans increased only marginally by 0.1%. Among these, the growth of US dollar loans slowed to 1.8%, partly due to rising US dollar funding costs. For the full year of 2017, total loans recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Figure 4.10: Loan Growth. The growth in loans used in Hong Kong (including trade financing) declined from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major industries (Figure 4.11). Loan growth in the construction and property development and investment sectors slowed in the second half, partly due to authorities requiring banks to strengthen risk management on loans to property developers since June 2017. Although commodity trade and retail sales improved further, trade financing and transport sector loans recorded only relatively modest increases, while loans to the wholesale and retail sectors declined. In contrast, loan growth for financial and finance-related enterprises remained strong, reflecting to some extent the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Figure 4.11: Local Loan Growth by Individual Industries. Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with an increase of 5.0% in the first half. Within household debt, private loans (including credit card advances and other loans for personal use) accelerated further, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in private loans was mainly driven by borrowing from private banking and wealth management clients secured by financial assets. The growth of these loans was broadly consistent with the continued growth of client assets managed by banks. The risks associated with such secured loans are within a controllable range. Additionally, in January 2014, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks on risk management for private loans, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including setting caps on loan tenors and borrowers' debt-to-income ratios. On the other hand, although residential transaction volumes increased, the loan-to-value ratios for new mortgage approvals declined, and the growth rate of residential mortgage loans dipped slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the ratio of household liabilities to GDP rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Figure 4.12).

Retail banks' profitability improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016, primarily driven by growth in net interest income. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. After experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, credit growth moderated in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR), the cost of Hong Kong dollar (HKD) funding for retail banks remained low due to persistently low retail deposit rates. However, banks should remain vigilant against the risks of increased interest rate volatility and potential capital outflows under the normalization of US monetary policy, as well as geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and high personal debt burdens, banks should assess the potential impact of interest rate increases exceeding expectations on asset quality. To enhance banks' resilience to systemic risks, the counter-cyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% effective from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% year-on-year. This was primarily attributable to a substantial increase in net interest income and a reduction in loan impairment provisions, which more than offset a decline in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets (ROA) for retail banks edged down from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the ROA in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Figure 5.1). On a full-year basis for 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the ROA rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Figure 5.1 Profitability of Retail Banks The net interest margin of retail banks further widened from 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Figure 5.2). Observed evidence indicates that the improvement in net interest margin is consistent with the rise in the average spread on HKD corporate loans in Hong Kong's syndicated loan market (Figure 5.3). Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Figure 5.3 Average Spread on HKD Syndicated Loans Since September 2017, HIBOR has risen across the board, primarily driven by liquidity demands related to initial public offerings and year-end needs of banks, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. Among them, the 3-month HIBOR reached 1.31% at the end of December 2017, the highest level since the financial crisis, representing an increase of 53 basis points from the end of June, though it remains low by historical standards (blue line in Figure 5.4). Entering 2018, with easing year-end liquidity demands from banks, HIBOR appears to have stabilized. Despite the recent rise in HIBOR, the cost of HKD funding for retail banks has remained stable. This is mainly due to persistently low retail deposit rates during the review period. Under these circumstances, the composite rate reflecting the average cost of HKD funding for retail banks remained at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, rising only slightly to 0.38% by the end of December (green line in Figure 5.4). A similar trend was observed in the overall HKD and US dollar (USD) funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average non-deposit market funding costs for HKD and USD rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding costs increased slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total funding costs for HKD and USD for licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Figure 5.5). Figure 5.4 Interest Rates Figure 5.5 HKD and USD Funding Costs and Tenors of Licensed Banks The rise in HIBOR exceeded the overall funding cost increase for the Hong Kong banking sector, which may help improve the margins on assets benchmarked to HIBOR. However, this improvement could be partially offset by intense competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market data indicate that some banks have reduced the spread between their mortgage rates and benchmark rates or introduced fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater pressure from rising funding costs. In view of the intense competition in the loan market, if the increased funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could exert pressure on banks' net interest margins. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remains well above international minimum standards, indicating that Hong Kong's banking sector maintains strong capitalization. As of the end of December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at the end of June to 19.1% (Figure 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Figure 5.6 Capital of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) recently published a consultation paper to seek views on the formulation of rules on loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions helps reduce the likelihood of financial crises, thereby benefiting society, it will inevitably entail costs. Feature 5 conducts a cost-benefit analysis of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements will bring net benefits to the Hong Kong economy. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average LCR of Class 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) of Class 2 institutions declined slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter to 49.4% in the fourth quarter of 2017, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions demonstrates that Hong Kong's banking sector can withstand liquidity shocks resulting from potential capital outflows from Hong Kong. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The NSFR, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce banks' medium- to long-term funding risks by mandating that banks maintain sufficient stable funding sources to finance their business activities. Specifically, Class 1 institutions must maintain an NSFR of not less than 100% at all times. Customer deposits remain the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure within the banking system. As of the end of December 2017, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged from six months earlier, at 56.2% (Figure 5.8). Figure 5.8 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 77.1% at the end of June 2017 to 82.7% at the end of December (Figure 5.9), reflecting that the growth in HKD loans and advances outpaced that of deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposit growth exceeded loan growth, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined from 65.5% at the end of June 2017 to 63.1% at the end of December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio calculated across all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of the rising loan-to-deposit ratio on their liquidity management. Figure 5.9 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a low level. We estimate that under a shock scenario of a 200-basis-point parallel rise in interest rates, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base as of the end of December 2017 (Figure 5.10). Nevertheless, given the expectation that the US Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalization, banks should assess the impact of this situation on their interest rate risk management. Figure 5.10 Impact of Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks In the second half of 2017, against a moderate yet favorable economic backdrop, the growth rate of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed from a robust 10.2% in the first half to 5.3%. Following two years of moderating growth, total loans grew steadily by 16.1% for the full year of 2017. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. As of the end of December 2017, the total specifically classified loans ratio and the overdue and restructured loans ratio of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52%, respectively, from 0.84% and 0.61% at the end of June. For retail banks, the total specifically classified loans ratio and the overdue and restructured loans ratio also declined to 0.54% and 0.4%, respectively (Figure 5.11). However, given the rapid growth in loans utilized outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may become more sensitive to external conditions; therefore, banks should closely monitor their credit risks. Figure 5.11 Asset Quality of Retail Banks As banks have become more optimistic about near-term credit growth, the strong credit growth is expected to persist. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" conducted in December 2017 showed that 29% of surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to grow in the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk for personal loans remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolios remained sound, with the delinquency rate staying at a low 0.03% as of the end of December 2017. The average loan-to-value (LTV) ratio for newly approved mortgages further declined from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.12). The global economy continued to grow, but the growth momentum weakened due to persistent trade frictions, tighter financial conditions, and other special and cyclical headwinds that increased uncertainties. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," leading investors to rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. However, financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary tightening, such as rising US inflation. In Hong Kong, although the weak-side conversion guarantee was triggered in March, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. In the second half of 2018, the growth rate of total loans narrowed slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid headwinds including the ongoing US-China trade conflict and a slowdown in global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with a significant drop in transaction volumes and a decline in property prices, followed by signs of stabilization in early 2019. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector faces multiple headwinds due to increased uncertainties in the external environment. If these uncertainties intensify and persist over the long term, they could significantly dampen business confidence and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressure on bank profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should prudently assess the impact of a potential deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans.  In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy remained robust, growth momentum in other regions slowed. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major euro area countries saw slower growth and low inflation. A slowdown in global trade and a significant drop in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds for emerging market economies. In light of the slowing global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund lowered its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared to its October 2018 projections. Due to dimming growth prospects and escalating trade frictions, global stock markets experienced significant volatility at the end of 2018. The US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels unseen since the global financial crisis, raising concerns about an impending US recession. Nevertheless, the US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a recession in the short term remained low. Despite this, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainties. In the US, while moderate inflation provided the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, its data-dependent policy stance also signaled that financial markets may become more sensitive to upcoming data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary tightening, such as rising US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, whether a solution to avoid a "hard Brexit" can be achieved remains unknown. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilized due to a slowing appreciation of the US dollar and market expectations of a Fed pause on rate hikes; however, a deterioration in the external environment could drag down regional economic growth. In fact, the weakening momentum in global trade growth has already dragged down economic growth in several East Asian economies, and inflationary pressures have also eased. While this shift may alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private-sector debt levels in some countries remain severe. As detailed in Feature 1 (page 16), another challenge facing the East Asian region is that if the Federal Reserve's monetary policy changes in an unexpected manner, the resulting shock could spill over into the sovereign bond markets of emerging market economies, including those in East Asia.  In mainland China, growth further slowed in the second half of 2018 due to increased uncertainties in the external environment and a slight slowdown in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain in the absence of results from US-China trade negotiations. Due to a significant contraction in shadow financing activities, financing difficulties for private enterprises (particularly small companies) have increased over the past few quarters. Coupled with weakening economic confidence, this may also place pressure on business activities. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers must continue to strike a balance between stabilizing the economy and preventing potential systemic risks by adopting loose but targeted measures (such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts). At the same time, authorities have also implemented more supply-side measures to boost productivity growth (such as promoting competition among companies of different ownership types) and to provide better social safety nets for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 was also adjusted downward from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%.  In 2018, risk aversion dominated mainland China's financial markets. Bank asset quality deteriorated slightly during the review period, and the leverage levels of listed non-financial companies rose marginally. However, loan impairment provisions by banks increased further in the second half of 2018, and their risk exposure to off-balance-sheet wealth management products continued to decline; both developments helped protect the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was the further decline in leverage levels of listed companies in overcapacity industries—one of the main sources of bank credit risk—during the first three quarters of 2018. Feature 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors driving the recent improvement in business performance in overcapacity industries.  Compared with the first half of 2018, Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stagnated, and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging down full-year economic growth from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening economic activity was mainly due to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct and indirect impacts of the US-China trade conflict. The slowdown in private consumption growth may reflect increased economic uncertainties and the wealth depreciation effect resulting from adjustments in local asset prices. Externally, Hong Kong's goods export performance also deteriorated, particularly in the fourth quarter after the US and China implemented additional tariffs. Feature 3 examines in greater detail the impact of the US-China trade conflict on Hong Kong's goods trade performance and discusses the short-term outlook and associated risks.  Mainly due to the slowing global economic growth, economic growth is expected to slow further in 2019. Under the interplay of multiple factors, Hong Kong's export performance is projected to remain under pressure. Locally, with low unemployment and rising household incomes, private consumption is expected to continue supporting economic growth, although the outlook for overall investment expenditure may become more uncertain. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2019 to be between 2% and 3%, while the latest average growth forecast by private analysts stands at 2.3%. These forecasts are influenced by the various uncertainties and risks mentioned above.  Local inflation rose slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained at a moderate level. The slight increase in inflation was partly influenced by earlier growth in rents for newly signed local private residential leases. Meanwhile, although the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%, the lowest level in over two decades, signs of a slowdown in overall employment growth emerged. Looking ahead, as local economic growth momentum weakens, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2019.  Following the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee in late August, the HKD exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until the guarantee was triggered four more times in March 2019 (as of March 19). The HKD exchange rate appreciated in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades amid tighter liquidity. Entering 2019, the HKD depreciated against the USD, partly due to the rebuilding of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side conversion guarantee being triggered again in March, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. Due to the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee, the total balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of March 19). HKD HIBORs rose generally in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month HKD HIBORs rose by approximately 30 basis points to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). Entering 2019, HKD HIBORs declined overall due to waning seasonal demand. The composite interest rate measuring the average HKD funding cost for retail banks rose from 0.62% at the end of June 2018 to 0.83% at the end of January 2019. Given the rise in funding costs, following the upward adjustment of the US federal funds rate target range at the end of September, retail banks raised their prime lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. At the end of January 2019, the average mortgage rate for new mortgages followed the prime lending rate up to approximately 2.45%.  Due to persistent uncertainties related to US-China trade frictions and Brexit negotiations, fluctuations in capital flows may intensify. Additionally, the significant negative interest rate differential between HKD and USD rates may stimulate arbitrage trading activities, leading to capital outflows. In such circumstances, capital outflows and the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee are normal operations under the linked exchange rate system.  Since the beginning of 2018, both the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates faced depreciation pressures due to market concerns over an escalation of US-China trade frictions. However, buoyed by optimism from the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between the US and China, the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. Although US-China trade frictions continue, they have not yet had a significant impact on liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market. The overnight offshore RMB HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with RMB customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The daily average turnover of the Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system for RMB remained at high levels, rising further to RMB 1.0101 trillion in 2018. Despite lingering concerns over US-China trade frictions, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to continue expanding, driven by mainland China's capital account liberalization, the development of stock and bond connectivity mechanisms, and regional economic cooperation promoted under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Greater Bay Area strategy.  The local stock market has experienced roller-coaster movements over the past six months. In the early part of the review period, the market fell sharply due to continued tightening of US monetary policy, major divergences between the two sides in US-China trade negotiations, and increasing signs of a slowdown in mainland China's economic growth. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance. Meanwhile, during the trade war truce, China adopted more measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and open its markets to foreign investors. Although the US filed a highly politicized legal action against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides demonstrated a friendly posture, indicating a determination to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, the local stock market rebounded sharply at the beginning of this year. However, considerable uncertainties remain as both sides discuss the details of any agreement, and future developments in the US federal government's lawsuit could complicate the situation, particularly in the high-tech sector.  The HKD debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, and performance improved as market expectations strengthened near the end of the year that the pace of US monetary policy normalization would slow. Consequently, fund flows into bond funds reversed in the second half of the year and increased slightly. Hong Kong's offshore RMB market issuance rebounded significantly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as mainland companies continued deleveraging, total issuance remained below maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market still faces challenges, and its outlook depends on economic developments globally, particularly in mainland China.

During the review period, the global economy continued to grow, but the growth momentum weakened under the combined effects of specific and cyclical headwinds, particularly in regions outside the United States. In light of the dimming growth outlook, the Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasizing that decisions would be "data-dependent" and require "patience," and ceased providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. Given the Fed's data-dependent policy approach, financial markets may become more sensitive to data releases in the coming period and may perceive monetary policy as increasingly uncertain. Meanwhile, uncertainties surrounding global trade policies and escalating geopolitical risks could continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have remained largely stable since the end of 2018, owing to signs of a slowdown in the US interest rate hiking cycle and a stabilizing US dollar. However, the region may face a broad-based slowdown due to a deteriorating external environment, including the unresolved US-China trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies. In mainland China, growth momentum further slowed in the second half of 2018, and uncertainty regarding the growth outlook rose amid the US-China trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small and medium-sized enterprises. Consequently, policymakers adopted more targeted measures to stabilize the economy and support private and small enterprises. Facing these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to guard against systemic risks and supporting enterprises and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to expand broadly. However, although the US economy remained overall resilient, some signs of a slowdown emerged. There were also clear indications that growth momentum outside the United States had moderated. Several country-specific shocks, including natural disasters in Japan, the implementation of new vehicle emission standards in Germany, a sharp rise in Italian government bond yields due to a fiscal stalemate with the European Union, and social unrest in France, all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Figure 2.1). In addition, cyclical slowing in global import growth posed headwinds to industrial production in emerging market economies (Figure 2.2). A sharp decline in oil prices in the fourth quarter also brought new challenges to emerging market economies that are major commodity exporters. Given the moderation in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Figure 2.1: Composite Purchasing Managers' Index for Selected Advanced Economies. Figure 2.2: Global Imports and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies. In the fourth quarter, concerns over the sustainability of US corporate earnings growth, exacerbated by a slowdown in global growth momentum and heightened trade policy uncertainties, together with statements by the Federal Reserve indicating that monetary policy would continue to tighten, triggered a significant correction in global stock markets. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Treasury yield curve flattened to levels unseen since the global financial crisis, prompting some market participants to worry about an impending US recession (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3: Spread between 10-Year and 3-Month US Treasury Yields and the Probability of a US Recession. Nevertheless, the probability of a US recession in the near term remains low. The US economic fundamentals remain robust, particularly the tight labor market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. At the same time, the US output gap is estimated to have returned to positive territory only last year, making a significant tightening of monetary policy by the Fed to counter overheating less likely. However, possibly taking into account the substantial tightening of financial conditions since the fourth quarter, senior Fed officials began emphasizing in early January that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that moderate inflation pressures allow them to exercise "patience" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. Furthermore, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee ceased providing forward guidance on further rate hikes and announced that it "would consider adjusting any details of the balance sheet normalization in light of changes in economic and financial conditions." This shift triggered a rebound in global stock markets (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4: S&P 500, MSCI World (ex-US), and MSCI Emerging Markets Indices. Despite the Fed's recent dovish signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains highly uncertain, contingent on inflation and other developments. To date, inflation pressures have been moderate, giving the Fed room to proceed gradually with monetary normalization. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the view that "patience" can be maintained (Figure 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple adverse factors, including slower growth outside the United States and trade policy uncertainties. Given these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Figure 2.5: Market-Based and Survey-Based US Inflation Expectation Indicators. However, the tight labor market is expected to continue supporting overall US economic performance. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically implies that inflation could intensify in the future (Figure 2.6). Therefore, market expectations that effectively rule out Fed rate hikes in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Figure 2.7). Figure 2.6: Average Hourly Earnings and Core Personal Consumption Expenditures Inflation. Figure 2.7: Federal Funds Rate Target Range and Futures-Implied Probabilities of No Rate Hikes in 2019 versus At Least One Rate Hike. In summary, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is not inevitable. To minimize policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasized that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. This implies that financial markets may become more sensitive to subsequent data releases, particularly those that could prompt a tightening of monetary policy. Monetary policy outlooks for other major central banks are also uncertain. In the euro area, the European Central Bank terminated its asset purchase programme in December while continuing to reinvest the full principal of maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance to keep policy rates unchanged at least until summer 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, describing the risks to the growth outlook as "tilted to the downside." The implications of this downward revision for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan stated at its recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary amid rising downside risks. However, significant obstacles may exist to further monetary easing, as its effectiveness is questioned and the drawbacks of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for an extended period are becoming increasingly apparent; for instance, regional banks' capital ratios have fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018 due to persistently low yields dragging on profitability. Consequently, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the short term. In addition to uncertainties related to the global monetary policy outlook, unclear outcomes of future trade negotiations and escalating geopolitical risks constitute two major sources of risk to the global economic outlook. The US government announced in early December that it would not increase tariffs on imports from China for 90 days and extended this deadline again at the end of February, but whether both sides can reach a long-term trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the US and the European Union have made virtually no progress to date. Given the uncertainty surrounding these trade negotiations, they may continue to cast a shadow over the global economic outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also quite prominent. In the US, partisan disagreements over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from the end of December 2018 to the end of January 2019. Although the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, tensions between the Trump administration and the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives could lead to further policy stalemates in the future. In the UK, after Prime Minister Theresa May's Brexit proposal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, risks associated with Brexit and its knock-on effects surged sharply, and whether a solution can be crafted at the eleventh hour to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit" remains uncertain. Elsewhere, heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the US reimposing sanctions on Iran, could also introduce uncertainties to oil prices, thereby affecting the global growth outlook. In East Asia, after volatile performance in the first three quarters of last year, financial markets stabilized broadly in the fourth quarter. The US dollar has stabilized since October, and signs that the Fed is exercising patience regarding further rate hikes have eased pressures on currency depreciation and capital outflows faced by East Asian economies. Several regional currencies appreciated slightly against the US dollar in the fourth quarter, and securities investment capital flows returned to net inflows (Figure 2.8). Figure 2.8: East Asia: Currency Index and Capital Flows. Despite financial market stability, growing signs indicate that the region will face a broad-based slowdown. Due to the weakening global trade momentum caused by the US-China trade conflict, regional export growth declined, leading to a slowdown in real GDP growth for most East Asian economies in the second half of last year. In fact, the new export orders sub-index of the Purchasing Managers' Index for several regional economies (reflecting short-term external trade performance) has fallen into contraction territory since the fourth quarter, foreshadowing a further moderation in short-term growth momentum (Figure 2.9). Figure 2.9: New Export Orders Index of Markit Purchasing Managers' Index for East Asian Economies. In the environment of slowing growth, coupled with the recent decline in oil prices, inflation pressures in East Asia have eased (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: East Asia: Overall Inflation Rate and Oil Prices. Given that recent inflation pressures and pressures from a rising US dollar have been relatively moderate, East Asian central banks no longer face an urgent need to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy dilemma of balancing the promotion of economic growth with the containment of inflation and capital outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian countries remains high by emerging market standards, central banks continue to face challenges related to financial imbalances (Figure 2.11).

Hong Kong's economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting a slowdown in private consumption growth and weaker export performance amid the US-China trade dispute. With global growth decelerating, real GDP growth is also expected to slow in 2019. The territory's growth outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and the performance of the mainland economy. Inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain moderate in 2019, with the outlook facing both upside and downside risks. Economic activity in Hong Kong softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic momentum failed to sustain the strong pace of the first half, and the quarter-on-quarter growth rate of GDP turned slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the fourth-quarter growth rate at 1.3%, below the trend rate, dragging the full-year growth rate down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Based on the expenditure-based, seasonally adjusted volume index of GDP. Chart 3.1: Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components. The weakening of economic activity was primarily due to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct or indirect impacts of the US-China trade conflict. Private consumption growth likely slowed owing to heightened economic uncertainties and wealth-depletion effects arising from adjustments in local asset prices (Chart 3.1). Total investment expenditure declined significantly amid fragile business confidence. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly in the fourth quarter after the US and China implemented additional tariffs (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as the decline in total imports was faster than that in total exports, the net trade balance still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Feature 3 will examine Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance in greater detail and explore its short-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2: Real imports and exports. As economic activity weakened, job creation appears to have slowed in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to approximately 3,873,000 by the end of 2018, a lower increase than the 0.8% recorded in the first half of 2018. Due to weak output and employment growth, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no signs of significant improvement. Given further slowing of global economic growth, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to decelerate in 2019. Amid external challenges, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, although low unemployment and rising household incomes will continue to support private consumption, the pace of private consumption growth is expected to slow, partly due to weakened consumer confidence and wealth-depletion effects stemming from earlier asset price adjustments. Regarding gross fixed capital formation, the outlook may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to continue growing steadily as housing supply increases, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid rising economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators, such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index, continue to hover in contraction territory. Forecasts of future economic growth derived from this index suggest that the year-on-year increase in GDP will further decelerate in the near term. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2019 to be between 2% and 3%, while the latest growth projections by private analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is affected by the multiple uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding two chapters. Although domestic inflationary pressures have continued to build in recent months, they remain at a moderate level. On a year-on-year basis, the Core Composite CPI recorded increases of 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018, respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half. The annualised three-month Core Inflation Rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, also rose recently, from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight uptick in inflationary momentum was driven by increases in prices of certain services. Earlier growth in newly signed private residential rents and accelerating increases in dining-out prices continued to push up service inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures have remained broadly moderate over the last few quarters (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3: Various indicators reflecting consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4: CPI rent component and market rents. Chart 3.5: Unit labour costs and average wages per capita. Looking ahead, domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate in 2019, mainly reflecting weaker domestic growth momentum. However, the earlier upward trend in private residential rents will continue to be passed through to consumer price inflation. Market consensus forecasts an overall annual inflation rate of 2.2%, a moderate level, while the government forecasts a core inflation rate of 2.5%. The above inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate has remained at around 2.8%, the lowest level in over two decades (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the current near-zero output gap could turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressure on inflation. Conversely, if US-China trade tensions ease, leading to better-than-expected economic performance, this could push up domestic inflation. Chart 3.6: Unemployment rate. The US-China trade conflict intensified in the second half of 2018: the US imposed 25% tariffs on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from mainland China on July 6 and August 23, respectively. In response, mainland China imposed reciprocal 25% tariffs on equivalent US goods. On September 24, the US escalated further, imposing 10% tariffs on US$200 billion worth of imports from mainland China. Mainland China subsequently imposed 5% to 10% tariffs on US$60 billion worth of US goods in retaliation. Thereafter, the two countries engaged in negotiations to avoid further tariff hikes. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as a re-export hub between these two economies, the tariff increases were bound to have direct impacts on Hong Kong through trade channels. Therefore, the US-China trade dispute has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This feature reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and explores its short-term outlook. We also attempt to utilise more granular data to identify trade goods directly affected by the tariff hikes, thereby examining the impacts of the tariffs more closely. To analyse the impact of tariffs, we first extracted six groups of Hong Kong re-export data, each affected by the respective rounds of tariff hikes described in the previous section. In the first two rounds, the US mainly imposed tariffs on capital goods and semi-finished products, while mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment, and energy equipment. In the third round, the scope of affected goods expanded, covering more consumer goods. For brevity, we refer to the goods affected by these three rounds of tariff hikes as List 1, List 2, and List 3, respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focused on analysing the year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong re-exports, adjusting for seasonal factors. Additionally, readers should exercise caution when analysing data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was partially disrupted by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis results in this section should be regarded only as preliminary evidence of the impact of tariff hikes. Hong Kong re-exports with mainland China as the origin and affected by tariffs: Shortly after the tariff hikes, relevant goods re-exported from mainland China via Hong Kong to the US appear to have decreased significantly or slowed in growth (Chart B3.1). For example, re-export growth for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the tariff hikes, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. Moreover, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1: Value of goods re-exported from mainland China via Hong Kong to the US in 2018. Hong Kong re-exports with the US as the origin and affected by tariffs: In contrast, goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to mainland China showed varied performance (Chart B3.2). Re-exports for List 1 appear to have declined significantly within a few months after the tariff hikes but recovered towards the end of the year. Re-exports for List 2 remained broadly at negative growth levels throughout the year, while growth for List 3 appears to have been broadly stable. Chart B3.2: Value of goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to mainland China in 2018. Front-loading: Due to the time lag between the announcement and final implementation of tariffs (or simply the threat of tariff hikes), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods before the expected effective dates of the tariffs. In fact, some data and news reports indicate that such front-loading behaviour is quite common. Some private analysts also believe that such behaviour was partly responsible for the strong overall trade figures before the tariff hikes. More granular trade data show some signs of front-loading for certain tariff-listed goods, but this appears to have involved only goods re-exported from mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). Re-export growth rates for List 1 and List 2 rose in the months preceding the respective effective dates of the tariffs. On the other hand, growth rates for goods re-exported from the US via Hong Kong to mainland China (Chart B3.2) show no clear evidence of significant front-loading by businesses. Hong Kong re-exports not affected by tariff hikes: It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (in value) directly affected by the tariff hikes accounted for only about 4% to 5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete understanding of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by the tariff hikes. We found that re-exports not affected by the tariff hikes recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Additionally, the decline in growth of re-exports affected by tariffs (red line) has been significantly larger since the third quarter, reflecting the pronounced impact of the tariffs. The slowing growth of re-exports not affected by tariff hikes partly reflects broader weakening external demand. As trade frictions persist, leading to increased uncertainties, tighter global financial conditions, and rising geopolitical risks, external demand could be more broadly suppressed. In particular, trade conflicts have dragged down global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in adjustments in major stock markets. Import demand from other economies has consequently been dampened, suppressing Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3: Value of Hong Kong re-exports in 2018. Even if US-China trade tensions ease, the short-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global growth may slow in 2019 (see Chapter 2), which is likely to further dampen Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators show that businesses of all sizes are pessimistic about their business prospects (Chart B3.4), with business sentiment in the trade sector being particularly low. Other trade-related sectors, such as logistics, may also be affected. Chart B3.4: Survey on business prospects in Hong Kong's import and export industries.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate strengthened in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades due to tighter liquidity driven by expected seasonal funding demands. As 2019 began, the HKD gradually weakened, partly due to corporations repatriating proceeds from new share issuances and the market rebuilding carry trade positions, triggering the weak-side conversion guarantee in March. Nevertheless, HKD trading remained smooth and orderly. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US interest rate hikes and seasonal funding demands, before declining in January 2019. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, HKD capital flows may become more volatile. If the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US remains significant, carry trade activities may persist, keeping the HKD relatively weak over the coming period and potentially triggering the weak-side conversion guarantee again, which is consistent with the design of the linked exchange rate system. Following the activation of the weak-side conversion guarantee in late August, the HKD exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499 until March 2019, when the weak-side conversion guarantee was triggered again for a total of four times (as of March 19) (Figure 4.1). The HKD exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trades under tighter liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The HKD stabilized again from November onwards due to tighter liquidity driven by year-end funding demands, leading to the unwinding of carry trades. As 2019 began, the spot exchange rate weakened, partly reflecting corporate repatriation of new share issuance proceeds and the market rebuilding carry trade positions. With the interest rate differential between Hong Kong and the US widening after the year-end, market participants engaged in carry trades by buying US dollars and selling HKD, driving the HKD to gradually weaken and triggering the weak-side conversion guarantee again in March. Despite the activation of the weak-side conversion guarantee, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Aggregate balances have remained at approximately HKD 76 billion since August (Figure 4.2), declining slightly to HKD 70.9 billion after the weak-side conversion guarantee was triggered in March (as of March 19). Capital outflows from Hong Kong since April 2018 represent only a small fraction of the approximately HKD 1 trillion that has flowed in since 2008. Figure 4.1: HKD Exchange Rate. Figure 4.2: Capital Flow Indicators. The HKD nominal effective exchange rate index generally followed the US dollar and continued to rise during the review period (Figure 4.3). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the impact on the HKD real effective exchange rate index was limited, with its trend largely following that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Figure 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. The latest balance of payments statistics show that securities investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Against a backdrop of weak market sentiment and heightened equity market volatility, outflows of equity securities investments by local residents accelerated, more than offsetting inflows of securities investments by non-local residents in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investments by both local and non-local residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties such as the ongoing US-China trade friction, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalization, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the HKD and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activities, leading to capital outflows. Under the linked exchange rate system, the HKD exchange rate may weaken, and the weak-side conversion guarantee may be triggered again. Capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee are normal operations under the linked exchange rate system. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalization process and the repeated triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee from April to August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD monetary base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half, standing at HKD 1,632.9 billion at the end of 2018 (Figure 4.4). The contraction in the monetary base was mainly due to the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee in August 2018, which reduced aggregate balances from HKD 109.5 billion at the end of June 2018 to HKD 76.4 billion at the end of 2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The HKD monetary base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with aggregate balances showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee in March, aggregate balances declined slightly to approximately HKD 70.9 billion (as of March 19). Figure 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. Regarding broader HKD money supply indicators, the growth rate of money supply generally slowed in the second half, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial environment. The HKD broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half but only marginally by 0.1% in the second half (Figure 4.5). As the main component of HKD M3, HKD deposits showed little change compared to the end of June (Figure 4.6). Among HKD deposits, demand and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half; conversely, term deposits continued to record strong growth due to higher deposit rates. Analysis of corresponding assets indicates that the slowdown in HKD M3 growth was due to changes in bank capital and reserves (included in "net other items"). Figure 4.5: HKD M3 and Changes in Corresponding Assets. The growth rate of foreign currency deposits accelerated in the second half. Following banks' increase in preferential deposit rates for US dollars, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Figure 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits grew marginally by 1.4% in the second half, with RMB deposits continuing to grow. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% increase in the first half. Figure 4.6: Deposit Growth. Although the HKD monetary base and deposit size remain substantial, the HIBOR began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US interest rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demands occasionally pushed up short-term HIBOR, resulting in greater volatility compared to long-term HIBOR (Figure 4.7). The 3-month and 12-month HIBOR averaged 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December, approximately 30 basis points higher than the June averages. As 2019 began, HIBOR generally declined due to reduced seasonal demand. The 3-month and 12-month HIBOR averages fell to 1.65% and 2.39% respectively in February. Figure 4.7: HKD and USD HIBOR. The HKD yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly following the movement of the US dollar yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2018, the yields on 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong government bonds declined by 45 and 37 basis points respectively to 1.56% and 1.83% at the end of February 2019 (Figure 4.8).
