Figure 4.8: Government Bond Yields, Composite Rate, and Average Mortgage Rate for New Loans. During the review period, the composite rate, which measures the average HKD financing cost for retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit financing costs, the composite rate increased from 0.62% at the end of June to 0.89% at the end of December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at the end of January 2019 (Figure 4.8). Given the rising financing costs, following the increase in the US Federal Funds rate target range in September, retail banks raised their prime lending rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the US Federal Funds rate target range was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to their prime lending rates. On the other hand, the average mortgage rate for new mortgages followed the rise in the prime lending rate, standing at approximately 2.45% at the end of January 2019. Looking ahead, the trend in US interest rates, capital flows, and local financial market activities (such as new share subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of HKD interest rates. Given that the HKD monetary base remains substantial and the banking system holds a large amount of Exchange Fund Bills, and since banks can use these bills as collateral to borrow HKD funds at the discount window, the pace of rise in HKD interest rates should be moderate. Against the backdrop of intensifying US-China trade friction, both offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates depreciated against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Figure 4.9). However, amid optimism driven by the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between the US and China, offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates stabilized in November. Meanwhile, the spread between onshore and offshore RMB was not significant during the review period. Figure 4.9: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. Currently, the ongoing US-China trade friction has not had a major impact on liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market. Given that liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight offshore RMB HIBOR remained below 4% for most of the review period, rising only occasionally due to seasonal factors (Figure 4.10). The 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR hovered around 4% from September to December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at the end of February 2019, possibly reflecting recent monetary easing measures introduced by the People's Bank of China. Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how the progress of US-China trade negotiations will affect liquidity in the offshore RMB interbank market in 2019. Figure 4.10: Overnight and 3-Month Offshore RMB HIBOR. Hong Kong's offshore RMB funding pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a slightly faster pace than the 2.6% increase in the first half, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB 657.7 billion at the end of 2018 (Figure 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by RMB customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than individual customer deposits. However, the balance of certificates of deposit declined further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively larger number of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Driven primarily by an increase in net interest income, retail banks' profits continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained robust. Reflecting upward pressure on the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) and retail deposit rates amid the normalization of US interest rates, the overall funding cost for retail banks in Hong Kong dollars rose significantly but remained at a relatively low level. Against a backdrop of external uncertainty, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nevertheless, signs of stabilization in credit growth emerged since November, and asset quality remained robust by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds due to persistent uncertainty in China-US trade relations, a slowdown in the global economy, an unclear pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels, banks should remain vigilant about the impact of a potentially further deterioration in the external environment on the credit risk of their related corporate loans. Retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit increased by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while the return on assets (ROA) rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Figure 5.1). This strong performance was primarily driven by a significant increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the rise in loan impairment provisions and operating expenses. For the full year of 2018, retail banks' overall pre-tax operating profit grew by 19.4%, and the ROA increased from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%. Figure 5.1: Retail Banks' Profits. The net interest margin for retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period last year (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks. This roughly reflected further US interest rate hikes and a decline in interbank liquidity in Hong Kong dollars following the triggering of the weak-side conversion guarantee in August 2018, as funding costs for Hong Kong banks continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the 3-month HIBOR rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Figure 5.3). As banks generally raised term deposit rates to secure long-term and stable funding, retail deposit rates in Hong Kong dollars also increased during the review period. Furthermore, following the US interest rate hike decision at the end of September, banks raised their prime lending rates and correspondingly increased their savings deposit rates. Given the rise in both wholesale and retail funding costs, the composite rate (a measure of the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks) increased from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained at a relatively low level by historical standards. Figure 5.3: Interest Rates. (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Average figures during the period for newly approved loans. On a broader front, the overall funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for licensed banks in Hong Kong continued to show an upward trend. In the second half of 2018, the average overall funding costs in Hong Kong dollars and US dollars for banks rose by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4: Funding Costs and Maturities of Licensed Banks in Hong Kong Dollars and US Dollars. The cumulative increase in HIBOR exceeded the rise in the overall funding costs for Hong Kong banks, which may have a positive impact on mortgage loans benchmarked to HIBOR offered by retail banks, a product that the industry has been actively promoting over the past few years. However, future improvements in net interest margins may become more limited, as most HIBOR-benchmarked mortgage loans have already reached the ceiling rate based on the prime lending rate. Given the uncertainty surrounding the timing of future increases in the prime lending rate, the continued upward trend in bank funding costs in the context of US interest rate normalization may weigh on the overall net interest margin. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cast a shadow over banks' profit prospects. Particularly against the backdrop of slowing global economic growth, persistent uncertainty in China-US trade relations may dampen business confidence and reduce demand for bank credit. Should this situation lead to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it may weigh on banks' profitability. The capital base of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong, well above international minimum standards. As of the end of 2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further rose to 20.3% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital. Figure 5.5: Capital Adequacy of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions. 1. Consolidated position. 2. From January 1, 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions have been required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Therefore, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards cannot be directly compared with data up to December 2012. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduced non-risk-based leverage ratio requirements to limit excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.0% as of the end of December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6: Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions. Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR for Type 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) for Type 2 institutions also increased from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Figure 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures. The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates the stable funding position of authorized institutions. The average NSFR for Type 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Figure 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Type 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and robust funding position of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector can withstand various liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. As of the end of 2018, customer deposits accounted for 55.7% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, a slight increase from 54.5% six months earlier (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9: Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions. 1. Figures may not sum to totals due to rounding. 2. Figures represent the percentage of total liabilities (including capital and reserves). 3. Debt securities include negotiable certificates of deposit and all other negotiable debt instruments. As the total amount of loans and advances declined in the second half of 2018, while the total amount of deposits increased during the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 75.7% at the end of June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Figure 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions declined from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, as the growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits was significantly lower than that in Hong Kong dollar loans, the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio rose slightly from 85.4% at the end of June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end. Figure 5.10: Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions. The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. We estimate that under a shock scenario of a parallel 200 basis points increase in interest rates, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base as of the end of 2018 (Figure 5.11). Nevertheless, given the uncertainty surrounding the pace of further US interest rate hikes, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Figure 5.11: Impact of Interest Rate Shock on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks. 1. The interest rate shock refers to a standard parallel 200 basis points shock to the institution's interest rate risk exposure. 2. The impact of the interest rate shock refers to the effect on the economic value of the banking book and trading book, expressed as a percentage of the bank's total capital base. Against the backdrop of persistent uncertainty in China-US trade conflicts, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, signs of stabilization in credit growth emerged since November 2018. On a half-year basis, the total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018 after increasing by 5.3% in the first half (Figure 5.12). This decline was due to a slowdown in the growth of local loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade finance) and a decrease in loans used outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% during the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the first six months. For the full year of 2018, the loan growth rate slowed significantly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%. Figure 5.12: Loan Growth. Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the short term. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" in December 2018 showed that among all surveyed authorized institutions, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged over the next three months, while the proportion of institutions expecting a decline in demand rose to 18% (Table 5.A). Despite a slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained robust. The total specific classified loan ratio and the overdue and restructured loan ratio for all authorized institutions declined slightly to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively as of the end of December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40% respectively at the end of June 2018. For retail banks, the total specific classified loan ratio decreased slightly to 0.50%, while the overdue and restructured loan ratio increased slightly to 0.32% (Figure 5.13). Both ratios are at low levels by historical standards. Figure 5.13: Asset Quality of Retail Banks. 1. Specific classified loans refer to loans classified as "substandard," "doubtful," or "loss." 2. Figures before December 2015 reflect the position of retail bank offices in Hong Kong and overseas branches. From December 2015 onwards, the scope of the figures was expanded to include retail banks' main overseas subsidiaries. On a half-year basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to a slowdown in the growth of personal loans (including credit card advances and other personal-use loans), which offset the rapid growth of residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As the nominal GDP growth rate in Hong Kong was slower than the growth rate of personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose slightly from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Figure 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak, which began in early 2020, has simultaneously impacted both demand and supply, posing a challenge to the global economy distinct from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have implemented stimulus measures since early March to counteract the economic impact of the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile, and global financial conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and local environments, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Against the backdrop of a relatively strong Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable aggregate balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. After a moderate rebound in the first half of 2019, the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half. The residential property market softened generally since mid-2019, though the trend was somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage levels and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios under scenarios where these risk factors may intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, the global economy has shown preliminary signs of stabilization, benefiting from major central banks increasing the intensity of monetary easing, a de-escalation of US-China trade tensions, and a reduction in the risk of a "no-deal" Brexit. However, since late January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has sparked market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have significantly cut interest rates and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid rising credit spreads and sharp declines in stock markets, global financial conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will dampen global economic activity, with the extent of the economic impact depending on the severity and duration of the outbreak. In the medium term, relations between the United States and its major trading partners may become tense again, and trade negotiations between the United Kingdom and the European Union following Brexit may also encounter significant difficulties. Weak global demand continues to weigh on economic growth in East Asia. Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. While some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported revenue growth, it remains to be seen whether there will be a broad-based rebound in the technology product cycle. Financial markets reacted positively to the Phase One US-China trade agreement announced in December 2019, and the trade truce has to some extent reduced uncertainties in global trade. Nevertheless, the East Asian region will continue to face adverse factors such as weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that the regional economy could face further pressure amid continued weak growth. Travel bans implemented by multiple economies in the region may impact Asia's tourism industry, particularly those economies more reliant on tourism service exports. Given the close supply chain links between the region and mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade agreement between the US and China helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the mainland economy, downside pressures remain due to the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the impact of a slowing global economy. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 identified economic stability as a priority for 2020, while also emphasizing the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecast indicates that mainland China's economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, especially small and medium-sized private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced declining shareholders' equity in recent years, which is seen as a sign of "retreat of the private sector." Special Feature 2 examines the drivers of changes in equity of mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more prone to downsizing or "retreat." Although the study found that negative profits were the largest driver, other factors, especially structural ones, also warrant attention (see Special Feature 2 for details). Local economic activity in Hong Kong contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real gross domestic product (GDP) declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, a deterioration from the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. Slowing local demand, particularly a reduction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down local GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social events severely impacted consumer activity, leading to a weak economic outlook, which in turn reduced consumer and business confidence. With the resurgence of US-China trade frictions, slowing global economic growth, and a severe downturn in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. In view of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To provide banks with greater room to intensify support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic has recently introduced substantial downside risks. Since sectors such as retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, tourism, and transportation have not yet recovered from the damage caused by social events, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash handout to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantees for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, which will provide banks with greater room to intensify support for the local economy, especially for industries and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the pandemic. Based on an analysis of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumption and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. Regarding external factors, the Phase One US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, US-China trade relations, mainland China's economic performance, and local social events. The labour market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with a decrease in total employment, a rise in the unemployment rate, and a year-on-year decline in the real wage index. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social events and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further. Special Feature 3 will explore recent developments and the short-term outlook for the labour market in greater detail. Local inflation pressure continued to build up to the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to rising prices of fresh pork; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually slowed. Due to weak economic conditions, consolidation of private residential rents, and moderate imported inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the short term. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the core inflation rate at 2.5%. Supported by increased demand for the Hong Kong dollar related to stocks (including initial public offerings), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. Upon entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate further strengthened, partly due to robust IPO activity and partly due to liquidity tightening near the end of the year prompting the covering of short positions in the Hong Kong dollar. After the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, during the review period, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner, and no Exchange Fund note conversion guarantees were triggered. The aggregate balance remained stable at approximately HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity needs and an increase in capital market activities such as IPOs. Special Feature 4 examines how market concerns about future IPO activity affect the 3-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR). Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting banks' continued adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised interest rate caps determined by the prime lending rate, the average mortgage rate for new loans rose to around 2.6% in October; however, due to the reduction in the prime lending rate in the market since November, the average mortgage rate for new loans fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. Against the backdrop of a relatively strong Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable aggregate balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no significant outflow of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system was observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of a further deterioration of the coronavirus outbreak in the context of external uncertainties. Hong Kong possesses substantial foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system; the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to address capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, market expectations of a US-China trade agreement led to a strengthening of both offshore and onshore renminbi exchange rates, but since late January 2020, they have faced weakening pressure due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the later part of 2019, the offshore renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi; by the end of January 2020, the discount briefly widened, but the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool recovered slightly after a slight decline in the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Other renminbi businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with renminbi bank loans and renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong recording strong growth. The daily average transaction volume of the China Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) for renminbi remained at a high level of RMB 1.1339 trillion for the full year of 2019. Despite external uncertainties, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of mainland China's capital account, increased allocation of renminbi assets by international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Greater Bay Area" initiatives.

Towards the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilization, fostering market expectations of a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous rise in global coronavirus infections dashed these recovery hopes, deepening investor concerns about a global economic downturn and triggering sell-offs in global financial markets. To address the economic shock, major central banks and some governments introduced stimulus measures from early March. Given the spread of the pandemic, downside risks to global economic growth prospects have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 cast a shadow over the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag down regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism sector hit particularly hard. On the other hand, East Asia continues to face challenges of weak corporate earnings and elevated private-sector leverage ratios. Regarding mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the first phase of the trade agreement between China and the United States helped temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and global economic slowdown, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by authorities will provide some buffer. Under the influence of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth remained lacklustre in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilization in the final quarter (Figure 2.1), partly benefiting from earlier easing policies by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as a moderation in global trade tensions following the signing of the China-US "Phase One" trade agreement. Figure 2.1: Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. However, since the end of January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus cases and the subsequent economic impact have sparked market concerns, leading to a sell-off wave in global financial markets (Figure 2.2). Given that mainland China is a major global export destination and holds an important position in global supply chains, when the pandemic disrupts production activities there and drags down its economic growth, significant spillover effects will occur, potentially affecting the globe (Figure 2.3). Since the end of February, coronavirus cases have surged outside mainland China, which may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and bring direct risks to local economic activity. Figure 2.2: MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spreads. Figure 2.3: Exports of Goods and Services from Selected Major Advanced Economies to Mainland China in 2018 (Percentage of GDP). To address the potentially severe economic shock from the pandemic, some central banks (including the Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) cut interest rates from early March, while some governments also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face immense selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which may in turn exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4: Bloomberg Financial Conditions Index for Advanced Economies. Besides the development of the pandemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also loom over the global economic outlook. Particularly regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased following the conclusion of the first phase of the China-US trade agreement, subsequent negotiations may prove difficult given that many thorny structural issues remain unresolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to proceed smoothly, thereby prolonging uncertainties following Brexit. Additionally, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will place pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained lacklustre in the second half of 2019 due to weak global demand. Exports from East Asia to major destinations such as the United States, European economies, and mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Figure 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downturn cycle for regional technology products is bottoming out and recovering, including reports from major regional electronics companies that their earnings improved at the end of 2019, it remains to be seen whether a substantive rebound in regional technology product exports will materialize. Figure 2.5: East Asia: Commodity Exports to Major Destinations Remain Weak. Persistent weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation falling in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Figure 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea, having cut rates in the first half of 2019, lowered policy rates again in the second half, while the Bank of Thailand also cut its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Figure 2.6: East Asia: Gross Capital Formation. The outbreak of the coronavirus has raised concerns that regional economies may face further pressure amidst continued weak growth. As multiple economies in the region have implemented entry and exit restrictions on mainland China, the tourism sector has been hit first and foremost; economies more reliant on mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports have been particularly affected by this pandemic (Figure 2.7). The persistence and intensification of the pandemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to mainland China. Figure 2.7: East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists. In the short term, the pandemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be transient, but the actual situation will depend on the severity of the pandemic, its scope of spread, and the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. Meanwhile, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although market expectations indicate that corporate earnings will deteriorate in the short term (Figure 2.8), the globally accommodative monetary environment encourages yield-seeking activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Consequently, regional stock markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Figure 2.8: Expected Earnings for Benchmark Stock Index Constituents. Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private institutions in the region to service their debts. Although declining local interest rates can provide breathing room for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as noted in Feature 1, as more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of debt accumulation for private institutions may also intensify, although this impact may be limited to enterprises with relatively sound financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowing. Third, regarding external factors, facing increasingly protectionist US trade policies, East Asian economies may face increased risks. Although progress has been made recently in the first phase of the China-US trade agreement, trade tensions between the two countries persist due to the continued existence of fundamental trade issues. As evidenced by the continuous increase in trade surpluses with the United States for multiple economies in the region (Figure 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to seek more supply channels outside China-centric supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus with the United States for nine Asian emerging economies (excluding China) had risen to approximately US$167 billion. If trade surpluses with the United States continue to expand, relevant Asian economies may become the next targets of the trade war; for instance, the US government imposed massive tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. In light of this, despite the China-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Figure 2.9: Goods Trade Surplus with the United States. Over the past decade, intensified integration of international financial markets has led to a significant increase in global cross-border securities investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-tracking funds. Index-tracking funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also funds that actively manage portfolios with reference to investment indices. By introducing overseas investors who were previously unable to attract or access these economies, these funds have helped promote the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. Thus, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to long-term market growth and stability. However, is there really such a thing as a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, market concerns exist that such fund investments may weaken the fiscal discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to high leverage levels for those companies. Additionally, there is an opinion that the growth of index-tracking funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global securities investment flows, making emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and influenced by other common factors, even more vulnerable. This feature evaluates the impact of index-tracking investments on financial stability based on these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to relevant bonds according to the weights of constituent bonds within the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions taken by passive bond funds may leave issuers of index-constituent bonds lacking the motivation to act in the interests of fund investors. Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may encourage excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and solvency risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, where leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Figure B1.1). Figure B1.1: Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies. Using the weights of enterprises in emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of their bonds' exposure to passive bond fund investment, we find that an increase in such investment will raise the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The blue solid bars in Figure B1.2 indicate the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base driven by passive bond funds also benefits the development of enterprises in emerging market economies. We also find that the aforementioned effects have a significant impact only on emerging market enterprises with relatively sound fundamentals (especially stronger solvency and lower leverage ratios) (green solid bars in Figure B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged or less solvent companies do not seem to fall further into a debt trap due to investment from passive bond funds. In summary, the above research shows that the growth of passive bond fund investment does not necessarily significantly increase solvency risks for the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Driven by weakening private consumption, declining investment expenditure, and poor export performance, Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the coronavirus outbreak recently introducing substantial downside risks. The economic outlook remains influenced by numerous uncertainties and risks, including slowing global economic growth, US-China trade relations, economic performance in mainland China, and the evolution of local social events. Given these various economic headwinds, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. While domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease, the outlook faces potential risks on both the upside and downside.  Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% in Q3 and 2.9% in Q4 (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the contraction in the second half of the year, the economy shrank by 1.2% for the full year, a deterioration from the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the 2009 global financial crisis.  Figure 3.1: Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components  On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed significantly in the second half of the year (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4% in Q2, 3.0% in Q3, and 0.3% in Q4, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the primary factor dragging down GDP in Q3. Local social events severely impacted consumption activities, weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer confidence, leading to a significant contraction in private consumption starting in Q3. 33 Due to increased economic uncertainty and a deteriorating business climate, total investment expenditure remained weak, weighing down GDP in Q4. 34 Externally, amid escalating US-China trade tensions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to languish (Figure 3.2). 35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in service exports, net exports weighed down GDP in Q3 but provided support for GDP growth in Q4, partially reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance.  Figure 3.2: Real Exports and Imports  Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government launched multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on residents, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and sectors severely impacted, such as retail, food and beverage services, transport, and tourism. 36 To provide banks with greater room to intensify support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) announced on October 14 that the counter-cyclical capital buffer ratio for banks would be reduced from 2.5% to 2.0%, enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion in lending capacity to businesses, including SMEs.  Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, with the pandemic recently introducing substantial downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the damage caused by social events, the pandemic will deliver a double blow to these industries. However, a series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide assistance to households and businesses (particularly SMEs), including the distribution of a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantees under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 On March 16, 2020, the HKMA further reduced the counter-cyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0%, providing banks with greater room to intensify support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the pandemic.  Analyzing the components of GDP, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to remain relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects reach completion. Regarding external factors, the initial phase of the US-China trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the short term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to disruptions in regional supply chains and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance.  The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is influenced by the numerous uncertainties and risks described in the preceding chapters.  The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and the early part of 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among these, the unemployment rate in the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services sectors surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partially reflecting the severe impact of social events. 39 As economic momentum weakened, the total number of employed persons fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was primarily driven by the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in Q3. Looking ahead, in light of the weak economic outlook described above, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is very likely to rise further. Feature 3 will explore recent developments and short-term prospects for the labor market in greater detail.  Figure 3.3: Labor Market Conditions  Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up to Q3 2019, primarily due to rising fresh pork prices; subsequently, as economic activity weakened, inflationary momentum gradually eased. On a year-on-year basis, the Core Composite Consumer Price Index (Core CPI) grew by 3.3% in Q3, with the growth rate moderating slightly to 3.0% in Q4. The Core Inflation Rate, calculated as a three-month annualized rate to reflect inflationary momentum, also softened from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The easing of inflationary momentum resulted from reduced price pressures on several components of the CPI. Regarding tradable goods, while fresh pork price increases kept core food inflation notably high, price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained moderate. In the services sector, following the earlier moderation in private residential rent growth, the growth of the rent component in the CPI also showed a downward trend (Figure 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at moderate levels in recent quarters (Figure 3.6).  Figure 3.4: Different Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation  Figure 3.5: CPI Rent Component and Market Rents  Figure 3.6: Unit Labor Costs  Domestic inflationary pressures are expected to ease in the short term. Domestically, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private residential rents continue to moderate, the housing rent component of inflation should further ease. Externally, due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices, imported inflation is expected to remain moderate. Market consensus forecasts the overall inflation rate for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the government forecasts a core inflation rate of 2.5% and an overall inflation rate of 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to risk factors on both the upside and downside. On one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since Q3 2019, if the economic deterioration proves more severe than expected (for example, due to the persistence of the coronavirus outbreak), inflation could be further suppressed. On the other hand, if disruptions to fresh pork supplies become more severe, this could bring upward pressure on inflation.  Although the local economy slowed markedly, the unemployment rate remained at a low of 2.8%-2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It only rose more noticeably to 3.3% by the end of 2019 as social events persisted. Affected by the coronavirus outbreak, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. In this context, this feature analyzes recent developments and short-term prospects for the labor market, including an exploration of why the overall labor market remained relatively robust in the first three quarters of 2019 (with almost no change in the unemployment rate) and what this implies for future developments. It also examines risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that, partly due to the costs associated with adjusting labor demand, the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by approximately two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature explains why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% even when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in Q3.  Figure B3.1: Real GDP Growth Rate and Unemployment Rate  Regarding labor demand, although tensions in the US-China trade situation and local social events dealt heavy blows to employment in the trade and retail/tourism-related sectors respectively, several major sectors continued to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in finance, business, public administration, and social and personal services continued to grow in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained resilient, and financial activities related to fintech development and initial public offerings were very active. These factors may have helped support employment in the finance and business services sectors. Furthermore, public administration, social, and personal services sectors, including education, healthcare, and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of public administration, social, and personal services sectors to the economic cycle is relatively neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical factors.  Figure B3.2: Changes in Employment by Sector in 2019  Regarding labor supply, the labor force participation rate 40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rising unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 illustrates the various supply and demand factors influencing changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, an increase in the number of employed persons in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, the significant economic contraction in the second half led to a reduction in employment, exerting upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although the number of employed persons decreased during the recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped alleviate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019.  Figure B3.3: Factors Contributing to Changes in the Unemployment Rate  Some structural changes in the labor market are also noteworthy. In particular, an increase in the proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons as a share of total employment have declined in recent years to 6% and 1% respectively, while the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second-largest group in the total employed population (approximately 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may retain or hire more employees by adjusting the working hours of part-time staff. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partially reflecting a higher proportion of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate strengthened since October, with upward momentum intensifying in December, keeping the HKD at the strong end of the currency board peg range for several months. Strong demand for the HKD stemmed partly from equity-related demand and partly from the unwinding of HKD short positions triggered by tightening liquidity near year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus outbreak could exacerbate capital flow volatility amidst an uncertain external environment, Hong Kong's substantial foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system enable it to withstand capital outflow pressures without compromising local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the HKD, including initial public offerings (IPOs), the HKD exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, upward momentum for the HKD further intensified, with the exchange rate remaining at the strong end of the currency board peg range from mid-December through February. The strengthening of the HKD exchange rate was partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly to the unwinding of HKD short positions prompted by tightening liquidity near year-end. Following the Lunar New Year holiday, liquidity conditions eased, and the HKD exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, HKD trading continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor weak-side conversion guarantee was triggered during the review period, the total balances remained unchanged at approximately HKD 54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1: HKD Exchange Rate; Chart 4.2: Total Balances and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. The HKD nominal effective exchange rate index broadly followed the US dollar, rising slightly during the review period (Chart 4.3). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the HKD real effective exchange rate index, the latter's trend largely mirrored that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. When measuring capital flows in Hong Kong, two distinct yet interrelated concepts must be distinguished: (1) HKD capital flows; and (2) cross-border capital flows. HKD capital flows focus on the currency dimension of capital flows, aiding the assessment of monetary stability, particularly under the linked exchange rate system. In contrast, cross-border capital flows focus on the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong's banking system, aiding the assessment of the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. These two concepts require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD capital flows, attention should be paid to the HKD exchange rate and total balances. If the public or investors significantly convert their HKD assets into foreign currency assets, demand for the HKD naturally declines, leading to a weaker HKD exchange rate. Under the linked exchange rate system, if the HKD exchange rate weakens to the weak-side conversion guarantee rate of HKD 7.85 to USD 1, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) stands ready to purchase HKD upon banks' requests, thereby reducing total balances. Since April 2019, total balances have remained broadly unchanged, and the HKD exchange rate has been at the strong end of the currency board peg range in recent months; thus, no significant outflow from HKD was observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border capital flows, the total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. Significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system would inevitably lead to a decline in bank deposits. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border capital outflows. Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on Hong Kong's monetary environment remained limited. However, risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak require close monitoring. With substantial foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA possesses the capacity, resources, and determination to manage capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite an uncertain external environment and a slowing local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively loose during the review period. The HKD monetary base remained substantial, rising 4.0% from the end of June to HKD 1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the conversion guarantee was not triggered during this period, total balances remained broadly unchanged at approximately HKD 54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and currency notes and coins issued by the government, rose steadily. Chart 4.4: Components of the Monetary Base. During the review period, broad HKD monetary supply indicators remained broadly stable. Broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, followed by a slight increase of 0.2% over the seven months since the end of June 2019. Corresponding asset analysis indicates that the growth in HKD M3 since the end of June primarily reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since the end of June, HKD deposits (the main component of HKD M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among HKD deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting rising HKD deposit rates. Chart 4.5: Changes in HKD M3 and Corresponding Assets. Over the seven months since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), primarily driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits declined by 1.0% over the same period, with Renminbi deposits priced in HKD recording a slight decline. Overall, total deposits of authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Chart 4.7). Given that monthly monetary statistics may fluctuate due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demands, as well as business and investment-related activities), these statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6: Authorized Institutions' Deposits by Currency; Chart 4.7: Total Broad Money Supply (M2). Although the monetary environment remained relatively loose, short-term HKD interbank offered rates (HIBOR) experienced volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demands and increased capital market activity since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly heightened IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market. The overnight HIBOR exhibited significant volatility in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally rose. Large IPO subscriptions exerted significant pressure on the overnight rate; Topic 4 presents empirical analysis showing that market attention to future IPO activity also affects the three-month HIBOR. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large IPOs and prepare medium-term funds in advance. Chart 4.8: HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates. Regarding the HKD yield curve, it shifted downward in line with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds declined by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9: Government Bond Yields, Composite Rate, and Average New Mortgage Rate. At the retail level, the composite rate, reflecting the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks' continued adjustment of preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, leading to a rise in the HKD weighted deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the Federal Reserve's reduction of the target range for the federal funds rate, several retail banks lowered their prime lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, retail banks' prime lending rates currently range between 5.00% and 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for mortgages pegged to HIBOR, major banks raised the interest rate caps determined by the prime lending rate, causing the average new mortgage rate to rise to around 2.63% in October. Since November, the prime lending rate in the market has been lowered, and the average mortgage rate subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity and to support the Federal Reserve in achieving its policy objectives, the Fed lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on 3 March and 15 March (US time). Although HIBORs generally follow US interest rate movements in the long term, short-term HIBORs may be influenced by local factors affecting HKD demand, such as local IPO activity. Total balances in the banking system have declined since April 2018, potentially increasing the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in HKD fund supply and demand. However, this does not imply that the current total balances level of HKD 54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, Hong Kong's interbank market has operated in an orderly manner. Should short-term liquidity tightness occur, banks can utilize the liquidity arrangements provided by the HKMA. Given the possibility of escalating US-China trade tensions, offshore and onshore Renminbi (RMB) exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with offshore RMB against the US dollar falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 on 2 September (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations of resumed US-China trade negotiations reversed the RMB depreciation trend; offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter and briefly breached the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the first phase of the US-China trade agreement. However, since late January, offshore and onshore RMB have again faced downward pressure due to the outbreak of the coronavirus. Offshore RMB traded at a discount to onshore RMB for most of the period from May to August, largely at a premium in the latter part of 2019, and the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020; however, the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10: Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates. Despite fluctuations in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the three-month offshore RMB HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to the MSCI A-share adjustment and near the Lunar New Year holiday at the end of January 2020.

Amid increasing uncertainties in the global and local economic environments, profits of Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, by international standards, the capital and liquidity positions of Hong Kong's banking sector remained strong and sound. Asset quality remained at healthy levels by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it remained faster than deposit growth over the review period. Accordingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios in all currencies and in Hong Kong dollars for all authorized institutions both rose. However, given that aggregate balances in the banking system remained at stable levels and deposits were largely steady, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, future China-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social events. Given the continuing rise in corporate leverage levels and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact of these risk factors, should they intensify, on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Accordingly, the return on assets declined slightly to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Figure 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.2), net interest income of retail banks continued to register moderate growth over the review period. However, loan impairment provisions and operating expenses of retail banks both increased, leading to a slight decline in profits. Figure 5.1: Profits of Retail Banks. Figure 5.2: Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks. Despite three 25-basis-point cuts to the US federal funds target rate in the second half of 2019, no significant downward pressure has yet emerged in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market. Instead, influenced by various local factors—including seasonal funding demands, increased liquidity needs due to large initial public offerings, and tighter liquidity conditions in the interbank market—short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, over the review period, longer-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates remained broadly stable, with the three-month Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) ending 2019 at 2.43%, close to the level six months earlier (blue line in Figure 5.3). At the retail level, given that Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, retail banks had limited room to follow the US policy rate cuts. On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened over the review period, banks continued to compete to attract stable long-term deposit funding. Reflecting an increase in the weighted cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months earlier to 1.09% by the end of 2019, though it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3: Interest Rates. From a broader perspective, given that the decline in US dollar funding costs for licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight rise in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs for licensed banks in Hong Kong fell slightly by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Figure 5.4). Over the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in overall funding costs and from relatively high Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates, thereby supporting banking sector profits during the same period. Figure 5.4: Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Funding Costs and Maturities for Licensed Banks. 1. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk framework within the banking book have submitted returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. Overall funding costs and maturities have been calculated as weighted averages based on the relevant figures for these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures since June 2019 are not directly comparable with those of previous months. Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environments will continue to cast a shadow over banks' profit prospects. Relevant factors include uncertainties stemming from the spread of the coronavirus, the trajectory of future China-US trade relations, and intensifying geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors could dampen already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low-interest-rate environment may persist, which could exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social events since mid-2019 have continued to undermine business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even intensifies in the future, it could lead to a deterioration in credit demand prospects and bank asset quality. In terms of overall market development, following the issuance of eight virtual bank licenses by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to launch virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by attracting new customers through more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates, this could exert upward pressure on the funding costs of existing banks. Although the short-term impact may remain moderate given the currently limited business scale of virtual banks, their long-term impact may depend on whether existing banks accelerate the adoption of financial technology to maintain competitiveness. The findings of Special Topic 5 show that the extent of financial technology adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and higher profitability levels. The capital base of Hong Kong's banking sector remains sound and well above minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further rose to 20.7% (Figure 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. Figure 5.5: Capital of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions. In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III includes a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to curb excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a sound level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6: Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions. Measured against the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound over the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio for Class 1 institutions rose from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio for Class 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%. Figure 5.7: Liquidity Coverage Ratio. The Net Stable Funding Ratio, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates the stability of authorized institutions' funding positions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio for Class 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Figure 5.8), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio for Class 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, exceeding the applicable statutory minimum of 75% for 2019. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector can withstand various liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8: Net Stable Funding Ratio. Customer deposits remain the primary funding source for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure in the banking system. At the end of 2019, the proportion of customer deposits in total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, falling slightly from 56.4% six months earlier to 56.3% (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9: Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions. The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio for all authorized institutions rose from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.10), as Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits declined slightly over the review period. Meanwhile, as the growth rate of foreign currency loans exceeded that of deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies for all authorized institutions rose from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% by the end of the year. Given that aggregate balances in the banking system have remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have been largely steady, there were no obvious signs of significant outflows of funds from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system over the review period. Figure 5.10: Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions. Interest rate risk exposures of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at relatively low levels in the fourth quarter of 2019. We estimate that, under a shock scenario of a 200-basis-point rise in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11: Impact of Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks. Against the backdrop of strained China-US trade relations, a slowing global economy, and ongoing local social events, bank credit growth, which had rebounded moderately in the first half of 2019, slowed in the second half. On a half-year basis, loan growth (measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) increased moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, then slowed to 2.4% in the second half (Figure 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to a deceleration in the growth of both local loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans used outside Hong Kong during the review period. Local loans and loans used outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the full year of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than 4.4% for the full year of 2018.

The launch of vaccines against the novel coronavirus has brought hope for economic reopening and bolstered global growth prospects. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, financial markets have reached new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, with recovery expected to be uneven across economies. In the medium term, the divergence between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the long-term scarring of the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner.
