The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side conversion rate, primarily driven by demand related to equities. During the review period, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partially reflecting weak economic activity and reduced credit demand due to recurring pandemic outbreaks, total bank lending declined slightly in the second half of the year, though a modest increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties regarding the pace of economic recovery and ongoing geopolitical risks will continue to challenge the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic weakens the repayment capacity of businesses and households, the banking sector must remain vigilant regarding the impact of these downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies worldwide reopened, but with a resurgence of novel coronavirus infections from the fourth quarter onwards, global growth slowed again. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development by the end of 2020, market expectations were that the pandemic would eventually end, facilitating a return to normalcy and accelerated growth for the global economy. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. In this context, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. Meanwhile, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies could lead to inflation higher than expected, prompting central banks to reduce monetary easing ahead of schedule, thereby ending financial market expectations of a "lower-for-longer" monetary policy. In the long run, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address numerous lingering economic issues triggered by the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and long-term economic scarring. In East Asia, domestic GDP growth improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in export demand. With increased risk appetite, inflows of securities investment funds into the region rebounded, and yield-seeking activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces ongoing uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less-developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, variables in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, combined with weakening fiscal positions of regional governments, could dampen market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. As for mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. For the full year of 2020, mainland China's economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will still largely depend on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in China-US relations. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that mainland China's economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months in early 2020 but strengthened for the remainder of the year, driven by an accelerating economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and strong capital inflows into the mainland bond market. Detailed studies show that during the novel coronavirus outbreak, fundamental factors, rather than market sentiment, played a more significant role in driving renminbi exchange rate fluctuations (see Feature 1 for details). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained far below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in local demand and further expansion of goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rise in the third quarter, ending a contraction streak of five consecutive quarters. The year-on-year contraction of real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to approximately 3% in the second half. However, for the full year of 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record and the first time in history that two consecutive years of contraction were recorded, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. Latest data on GDP by sector indicates that consumption and tourism-related sectors contracted more severely than the overall economy under the pandemic. To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two further rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-Epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist affected industries and the public, and to enhance Hong Kong's pandemic response capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021-22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic消费券 and providing 100% guaranteed personal special loans for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the "Banking SME Loan Coordination Mechanism," announced in March 2021 the extension of the "Interest-only Repayment" pre-approval scheme to October of the same year, and extended the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity difficulties faced by some corporate clients. The novel coronavirus vaccine is expected to restore economic activities to normal, with the local economy projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), although the strength and pace of recovery will be influenced by numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and efficacy of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's goods and services exports, while the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the efficacy of their large-scale vaccination programs. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2021 to be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private analysts is 4.4%. Labor market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate continued to climb, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To address the worsening labor market, the Government launched the "Job Retention Programme" under the second round of the Anti-Epidemic Fund, providing time-limited wage subsidies (June to November 2020) to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the "Job Retention Programme," the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund to further support industries severely hit by the pandemic. In the short term, due to weak economic conditions, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure. Feature 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of the visitor tourism industry on the local labor market. Local inflationary pressure continued to ease over the eight-month period from mid-2020 to February 2021. The core consumer price inflation rate declined significantly year-on-year to 0.3% in the third quarter of 2020 and 0.2% in the fourth quarter, falling further to -0.5% in January 2021 and -0.1% in February. Although the core inflation rate on a three-month annualized basis, which reflects inflationary momentum, fluctuated slightly in recent months, it remained at a low level. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressure in Hong Kong is likely to remain mild in the short term, particularly as local inflation will continue to be contained by the earlier slowdown in growth of newly signed private residential rents. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2021 at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts core and overall inflation rates for 2021 at 1.0% and 1.6%, respectively. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side conversion rate, primarily driven by equity-related capital demand, including from robust initial public offering activities and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect schemes. Fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar firm. During the review period, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with capital inflows totaling HK$263.3 billion. For the full year of 2020, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 85 times in total, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the pandemic's evolution, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing tensions in China-US relations may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, enabling it to withstand such volatility. With the triggering of the strong-side conversion rate increasing the aggregate balance, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates generally remained at very low levels. The composite interest rate, reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Due to lower funding costs, the average mortgage interest rate for new loans also declined from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. With the strengthening of the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore renminbi (CNH) appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi exchange rate traded at a premium to the onshore rate, with an average premium of about 100 basis points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020; as of the end of January 2021, the balance of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 826.3 billion. Regarding other renminbi businesses, renminbi bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while renminbi trade settlement grew, and the daily average transaction volume of the renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement system remained at a high level of RMB 1.1915 trillion throughout 2020. Hong Kong possesses efficient financial infrastructure, offering investors numerous cross-border channels for capital flows connecting to the mainland. With the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Greater Bay Area" initiatives, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit. Supported by rising global stock markets and active purchases of HK-listed stocks by mainland investors via Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a significant adjustment at the beginning of the review period. The rise in global stock markets was driven by unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism regarding positive progress in vaccine development, which could help accelerate economic recovery; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. In this context, the Hang Seng Index regained lost ground after a sharp decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the review period and briefly breaking the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, reaching a 32-month high. Supported by a stable issuance volume, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore renminbi bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. Following a large net outflow of funds in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered swiftly as governments worldwide introduced unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in bond fund inflows into the local market. Although bond yields experienced a mild rebound during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, remained hovering near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, market expectations have risen that the novel coronavirus pandemic will eventually end, allowing the global economy to accelerate its growth. Coupled with the anticipated "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors did not retreat despite the pandemic resurgence at the end of 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the fervent expectations in financial markets are disconnected from the macroeconomic environment, which remains fraught with challenges. Should the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance, due to inflation exceeding forecasts), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the difficult task of determining when to withdraw policy support and addressing numerous issues left by the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and long-term economic scarring. The ongoing uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over economic recovery in East Asia, where emerging market economies with slower development may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any stagnation in vaccination programmes could reverse current optimism, making capital inflows and financial markets unstable. In mainland China, as consumption activities gradually return to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, largely depending on the evolution of the pandemic and changes in US-China tensions. Consequently, the government announced its intention to maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by economic reopening, major economies mostly recorded real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020 that was better than expected. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of novel coronavirus infections has risen again, prompting governments worldwide to reimpose lockdowns and social distancing measures, thereby weakening the momentum of global growth once more. By the end of 2020, more contagious variants emerged and subsequently spread globally, exacerbating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use by the end of 2020, market expectations remain that the pandemic will eventually end, allowing the global economy to return to normal and accelerate growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery is continued policy stimulus measures, including the commitment by major central banks to "lower for longer" monetary policy amidst weak inflation, and ongoing fiscal easing measures in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raised its forecast for global GDP growth in 2021 to 5.5% in January 2021, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from its October 2020 forecast (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts Made in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, driving up stock prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery, which in turn propelled global stock prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Figure 2.2). Figure 2.2: 12-Month Forward Price-to-Earnings Ratios of Major Stock Indices. However, while financial market performance has been robust, the macroeconomic landscape remains challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amidst multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depends on whether vaccines can be widely distributed, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the global overall vaccination rate remained low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms (such as COVAX) facilitate a fairer distribution of vaccines, the issue of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe due to limited vaccine supplies. If pandemic control falls short of expectations, social distancing and other restriction measures may need to be extended in various regions, thereby undermining global recovery prospects. Figure 2.3: Population Percentage Receiving at Least One Dose of Vaccine in Selected Economies (as of March 15, 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is built upon continued monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn faster than expected. For instance, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong currency appreciation, liquidity growth, and active fiscal easing policies, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already intensified (Figure 2.4). If future inflation proves stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back the magnitude of monetary easing, and inflation data exceeding expectations could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Figure 2.4: 5-Year/5-Year Breakeven Inflation Swap Rates for the US and Eurozone. Third, there is significant uncertainty regarding future US-China relations. The wave of "decoupling" between the US and China, particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hardline attitudes of both the US Democratic and Republican parties toward mainland China, this trend is not necessarily expected to reverse under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in the US-China situation could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the difficult question of whether and when to withdraw anti-pandemic support measures. While withdrawing these measures prematurely could harm economic recovery and create a "cliff effect," these measures are costly in the long run, including imposing fiscal burdens and delaying the necessary reallocation of resources post-pandemic, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" with no longer viable business models to survive under continued government support. Furthermore, policymakers must also address numerous issues left by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government spending, global debt levels rose significantly in 2020 (Figure 2.5). Although the problems arising from the sharp rise in debt may not be immediate given the current extremely low global interest rates, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise concerns among markets regarding fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5: Global Debt as a Percentage of GDP. Another lingering issue involves potential long-term economic losses or scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, high uncertainty may cause businesses to reduce investment, while workers suffering from long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labour market, leading to significant waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of the year after a sharp decline in the second quarter of 2020 (Figure 2.6). The momentum for economic recovery primarily stemmed from a rebound in exports, with the strongest demand coming from electronic and technical equipment. Meanwhile, the service sector, which was hit hardest (such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face contact with customers), continued to struggle. Figure 2.6: East Asia: Real GDP Growth in 2020. Despite lingering uncertainties regarding economic recovery, securities investment funds have begun flowing back in. Since the second half of last year, improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds in advanced economies have attracted more bond fund inflows to the region (Figure 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the launch of vaccine production programmes, equity fund inflows into East Asia also accelerated in the last quarter of 2020. Regional currencies appreciated correspondingly due to securities fund inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Currency Index to rebound by approximately 10% from its low point in March of last year. Figure 2.7: East Asia: Securities Investment Fund Flows. East Asia continues to face ongoing uncertainties related to the pandemic. First, although the launch of vaccines has brought hope to the region's hard-hit service sector and economy, competition worldwide for early-batch vaccines has driven up procurement costs, while vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capabilities. Therefore, economies with slower development within the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closure periods and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, since investor optimism has been largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccination falls far short of expectations, the current capital inflows and rebound in financial asset prices could come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. As the novel coronavirus was successfully contained and consumption gradually recovered, mainland China's economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports also maintained growth, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical supplies and high-tech products) (Figure 2.8). Looking back at 2020, despite unprecedented shocks from the novel coronavirus pandemic, mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Figure 2.8: Mainland China: Contribution of Demand Components to GDP Growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecast indicates that mainland China's economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economy can continue to recover still depends, to a certain extent, on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in mainland China have normalized, the service sector remains partially disrupted due to new outbreaks in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to new waves of the pandemic in most developed economies. Furthermore, the tense situation between the US and China may not ease in the short term; however, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) signed earlier and the China-EU Comprehensive Agreement on Investment (CAI) reached could help China integrate further with other economies, potentially partially offsetting the adverse impact of US-China decoupling on economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains full of uncertainties, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo significant changes in 2021 to support economic growth, while simultaneously emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Additionally, the latest government work report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the long term, the 14th Five-Year Plan identifies technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy as priority development directions, aiming for per capita GDP to reach the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the novel coronavirus outbreak on the repayment capacity of bond-issuing enterprises appears to be limited, with the overall default rate in mainland China's bond market remaining at a low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a significant rise in defaults by state-owned enterprise (SOE) bonds, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Figure 2.9). Although the rise in SOE defaults primarily reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" of SOEs to promote more reasonable market risk pricing, limited fiscal space for some local governments may also be a contributing factor, particularly in less developed regions. Figure 2.9: Mainland China: Onshore Bond Default Scale and Proportion. In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, particularly for some high-risk issuers. Although the continued economic recovery and gradual normalization of interest rates contributed to rising financing costs for lower-rated issuers to a certain extent, several corporate default events in the last quarter of 2020 caused credit spreads to widen significantly (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: Mainland China: 5-Year Corporate Bond Yield. Regarding the real estate market, property prices in mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. In contrast, the pace of price increases in lower-tier cities was much slower (Figure 2.11). As for the issue of housing oversupply that plagued third-tier cities in previous years, it was basically under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales recorded in third-tier cities amidst high market sentiment. By the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities remained around 13 months, far below the peak of 31 months recorded in early 2015.

Although real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remains far below pre-pandemic levels, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 as local demand recovered and merchandise exports expanded further. With expectations that coronavirus vaccination will restore economic activity to normal, the economy is projected to resume growth in 2021 following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. Consequently, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the short term, while local inflationary pressure is likely to stay mild.  The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activity remained well below pre-outbreak levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. However, for the full year 2020, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and the first time in history that the economy contracted for two consecutive years, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest industry-level GDP data also show that the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in economic activity in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related industries contracting more sharply than the economy as a whole. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending a five-quarter downward trend (Table 3.A and Figure 3.1). Local private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, with the authorities re-imposing social distancing measures amid the third and fourth waves of the local outbreak, consumer confidence remained weak. As business sentiment briefly improved, overall investment spending also grew in the second half of the year. Partially benefiting from a stronger performance in exports, particularly to Mainland China, Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Figure 3.2). With the global tourism industry still in stagnation, trade in services remained weak. Overall, net imports (the trade deficit) weighed on GDP in the second half, partly reflecting that the recovery in merchandise exports was slower than that in imports. Figure 3.1: Real GDP Growth Rate and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components. Figure 3.2: Real Exports and Imports.  To address the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund, totalling HK$30.4 billion, between September and December 2020, to assist industries and residents affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's epidemic response capacity. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of one-off e-vouchers of HK$5,000 and fully guaranteed personal special loans for the unemployed. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the Banking Sector SME Loan Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 the extension of the "Pre-approved Interest-only Repayment" scheme to October of the same year, and also extended the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These deferral measures are expected to help alleviate liquidity difficulties faced by some corporate clients.  With the prospect that coronavirus vaccination will restore economic activity to normal, Hong Kong's economy is projected to return to positive growth in 2021 (for the full year), although the strength and pace of the recovery remain subject to numerous uncertainties, including the evolution of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the recovery pace of other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government projects full-year real GDP growth for 2021 to be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private analysts is 4.4%.  The labour market deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and in early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Figure 3.3). The underemployment rate also increased to 4.0%, the highest since the SARS outbreak. After falling to a low point, total employment stabilised (Figure 3.3), while government data show that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal average salary index for employed persons, a proxy for labour income, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To address the worsening labour market conditions, the Government launched the "Job Preservation Programme" under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. After the programme ended, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off allowances) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support industries severely affected by the pandemic. In the short term, given weak economic conditions, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure.
