As the coronavirus pandemic spread, the inbound tourism industry rapidly fell into depression, raising market concerns about a scarring effect on the future recovery of the labour market. To this end, this feature empirically analyses the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on the local labour market, thereby exploring the potential implications of the current tourism downturn. Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant fluctuations (Figure B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) outbreak in 2003. Following the introduction of the "Individual Visit Scheme" (IVS) in July of that year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, Mainland residents could apply individually for one or two visits per year, with each stay not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for a multiple-entry "Individual Visit" visa. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-border infrastructure connecting Hong Kong and Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social events halved visitor numbers in the second half of 2019, and under the coronavirus pandemic, inbound tourism has been in stagnation since the end of January 2020. Figure B2.1: Visitor Arrivals and Related Policies.  We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as a case study to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We regard the IVS, launched in 2003, as akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and unforeseeable by Hong Kong residents. Our main analysis draws on population data from the Hong Kong Population Census or the By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as catering, retail, accommodation, and transport.  First, we employ a "difference-in-differences" framework to compare differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41–65) in the "comparison group". We assign the younger cohort to the treatment group because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth of inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought by the IVS on the labour market may vary over time, we also employ an "event study" approach to identify time-varying effects.  Our empirical results show that, compared with the older cohort, younger workers (especially females and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. In particular, the IVS had a particularly significant and persistent effect on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries, remaining at a level close to five percentage points from 2006 onwards (relative to the average difference in entry probability compared with the older cohort) (Figure B2.2). We also used a similar approach to compare incomes between workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimates show that, after the implementation of the IVS, income growth for workers in tourism-related industries was higher than that for employees in non-tourism-related industries. Moreover, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and those with lower educational attainment in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising income increases (3–20 percentage points) (Figure B2.3). Figure B2.2: Impact of the IVS on Female Employment. Figure B2.3: Impact of the IVS on Incomes of Female and Low-Education Workers.  The above results are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that the tourism industry is an important source of employment, especially for young people, women, and workers with lower educational attainment. In Hong Kong's case, our findings also align with previous analyses, namely that strong growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled labour and enhanced the resilience of the labour market for lower-skilled workers. As inbound tourism has fallen from a boom to a trough, these labour groups may be more affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side conversion rate, which was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. Strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was primarily driven by equity-related funding needs, including robust initial public offering (IPO) activity and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Shanghai-HK Stock Connect and Shenzhen-HK Stock Connect). As the net settlement balance increased to over HK$450 billion, Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBOR) declined across the board. Despite uncertainties related to the development of the novel coronavirus pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and continued tensions in China-US relations, which could exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand pressure from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained close to the strong-side conversion rate, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including robust IPO activity and southbound capital inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Figure 4.1). Although some proceeds from initial public offerings were remitted overseas, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate fluctuated narrowly between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December, supported by a more buoyant local equity market sentiment and market expectations of rising funding demand towards year-end. With IPO activity remaining active during the first two months of 2021 (Figure 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar traded against the US dollar at 7.7568 on February 26, 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar transactions continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. During the review period, multiple triggers of the strong-side conversion rate led to an increase in the net settlement balance, reflecting substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 47 times. Under the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, increasing the net settlement balance from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion by the end of February (Figure 4.3). Over the full year of 2020, the strong-side conversion rate was triggered 85 times in total, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits indicates no signs of significant capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data show that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, with no indication of abnormal capital movements. Figure 4.1: Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Figure 4.2: Equity Funds Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange Figure 4.3: Net Settlement Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar generally declined, following the weakening of the US dollar against major currencies (Figure 4.4). Given the minimal inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, which had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the trend of the Hong Kong dollar's real effective exchange rate index largely followed that of the nominal index. Figure 4.4: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the pandemic's development, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing China-US tensions may intensify capital flow volatility. As an international financial centre, Hong Kong hosts various fundraising activities (such as IPOs), resulting in substantial capital inflows and outflows. On one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to shift funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong due to business needs. Hong Kong's ample foreign exchange reserves and sound banking system enable it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained loose in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base increased by 20.8% (Figure 4.5). By component, this increase reflected the rise in the net settlement balance resulting from multiple triggers of the strong-side conversion rate. Meanwhile, other components, including certificates of indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Figure 4.5: Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits derived from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (HKD M3) and its deposit components to rise significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Figure 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid their IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by the end of 2020. In January 2021, HKD M3 increased substantially again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO activities at the end of January. Overall, over the seven-month period since the end of June, HKD M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the end-of-January IPO activities, HKD M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Based on the corresponding asset analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HKD M3 was primarily due to the increase in the monetary base triggered by the strong-side conversion rate (Figure 4.7). As the main component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period; excluding the impact of end-of-January IPO activities, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although time deposits in Hong Kong dollars declined due to low deposit rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth of demand and savings deposits, partly driven by investment demand. Figure 4.6: Deposits of Authorized Institutions by Currency Figure 4.7: Changes in HKD M3 and Corresponding Assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits declined slightly by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits increased strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits of authorized institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Figure 4.6). Excluding the impact of end-of-January IPO activities, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demands, as well as business and investment-related activities), and thus should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the net settlement balance, HIBOR remained at very low levels overall during the review period (Figure 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HIBOR did not experience significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, Hong Kong's interbank market continued to function normally. Figure 4.8: HIBOR and US Dollar LIBOR The Hong Kong dollar yield curve generally followed the trend of the US dollar yield curve, becoming steeper during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Figure 4.9). Compared with the end of June, the yield on the 3-year Hong Kong government bond declined slightly by 4 basis points to 0.23% by the end of February, while the yield on the 10-year Hong Kong government bond rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% over the same period. Figure 4.9: Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rates, and Average Mortgage Loan Rates for New Loans At the retail level, Hong Kong dollar interest rates mainly declined in line with HIBOR. The composite interest rate, reflecting the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% by the end of February 2021 (Figure 4.9). Due to lower funding costs, the average loan interest rate for new mortgages also declined from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, largely following the trend of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given the prolonged low level of US interest rates, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demands. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffer to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened since the end of May (Figure 4.10), largely reflecting China's more favorable economic prospects compared to other regions and the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell's announcement at the end of September to include mainland Chinese government bonds in the World Government Bond Index further supported the renminbi's appreciation. For most of the review period, the offshore renminbi traded at a premium to the onshore renminbi, with an average premium of about 100 points in the fourth quarter, which remains moderate by historical standards. Figure 4.10: Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight offshore renminbi HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional northbound remittance demands and seasonal liquidity needs towards year-end, it remained below 4% for most of the time (Figure 4.11). The 3-month offshore renminbi HIBOR declined in late December, following onshore renminbi interest rates, and then rose again in late January, partly due to tightening onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Figure 4.11: Overnight and 3-Month Offshore Renminbi HIBOR Pricing In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi pool continued to grow. Since the fourth quarter, the growth rate of renminbi deposits accelerated, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and higher renminbi interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared with the end of June 2020, the growth of renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit accelerated, reaching RMB 826.3 billion by the end of January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Figure 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in corporate customer deposits. Meanwhile, the balance of certificates of deposit declined by 25.0% over the same period. Figure 4.12: Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong Regarding other renminbi-related businesses, over the seven-month period since the end of June 2020, the outstanding balance of renminbi loans decreased by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion. On the other hand, renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. Over the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions processed by local banks amounted to RMB 3,769.5 billion, a year-on-year increase of 16.7%. In these transactions, the increase in remittances from Hong Kong to the mainland was higher than that of remittances from the mainland to Hong Kong (Figure 4.13). Hong Kong's substantial renminbi pool is sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020, the average daily transaction volume of the Renminbi Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared to RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Amid the persistent economic downturn caused by the recurring novel coronavirus outbreak and compounded by the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, Hong Kong's retail banks recorded a further decline in profits in the second half of 2020, with a slight deterioration in asset quality. Nevertheless, given their continued strong capital and liquidity positions, Hong Kong's banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy through these challenging times, the HKMA decided to extend several relief measures. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may foster optimism that the global pandemic could be brought under control and economic activity resumed, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties, coupled with ongoing geopolitical tensions, are likely to adversely affect commercial activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic undermines the repayment capacity of businesses and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant regarding the impact of these related downside risk factors on asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020 from 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Figure 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.2), resulting in a decrease in net interest income that outweighed the slight growth in non-interest income, thereby leading to lower profits. For the full year of 2020, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, while the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Figure 5.1 Profit of Retail Banks Figure 5.2 Net Interest Margin of Retail Banks Largely driven by substantial capital inflows stemming from heightened stock market activity, HKD liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% by the end of 2020 (blue line in Figure 5.3). The trend of the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD funding cost of retail banks) was broadly similar, declining significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% by the end of 2020 (green line in Figure 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected lower interbank funding costs and rate reductions on time deposits by several major retail banks. Figure 5.3 Interest Rates From a broader perspective, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong moderated by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Figure 5.4). Figure 5.4 HKD and USD Funding Costs and Maturity of Licensed Banks Looking ahead, given that the global low-interest-rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on net interest margin performance, the profit outlook for the banking sector remains challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have bolstered market optimism regarding the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain due to considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors are expected to continue affecting the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capital position of Hong Kong's banking sector remains robust and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the international minimum requirement of 8% (Figure 5.5). During the period, the Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7%, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, surpassing the statutory minimum of 3% (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.5 Capital Adequacy of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Figure 5.6 Leverage Ratio of Locally Incorporated Authorized Institutions Measured against the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR of Class 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.7), significantly above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of Class 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Figure 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The most recent figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirement also indicate stable funding conditions for authorized institutions. The average NSFR of Class 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of Class 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Figure 5.8), significantly exceeding their respective statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75%. The abundant liquidity and stable funding conditions of authorized institutions indicate that Hong Kong's banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Figure 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remain the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure within the banking system. At the end of 2020, customer deposits accounted for approximately 56.1% of the total liabilities of all authorized institutions, similar to the level six months prior (Figure 5.9). Figure 5.9 Liability Structure of All Authorized Institutions As the total amount of deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020 while the total amount of loans decreased during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions, calculated in all currencies, fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% by the end of 2020 (Figure 5.10). The increase in total deposits largely reflected growth in both HKD and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, by the end of 2020, the average HKD loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio declined to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier. Figure 5.10 Average Loan-to-Deposit Ratio of All Authorized Institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200 basis point rise in HKD and USD interest rates, the estimated decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Figure 5.11). Figure 5.11 Impact of HKD and USD Interest Rate Shocks on Locally Incorporated Licensed Banks Against the backdrop of a persistent economic downturn caused by the recurring pandemic and tightened social distancing measures, the total amount of loans and advances registered a moderate decline in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, the banking sector still recorded positive growth in total credit, albeit at a significantly slower pace of 1.2% compared with 6.7% in 2019. On a half-year basis, the total amount of loans and advances of all authorized institutions, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, declined by 1.8% in the second half (Figure 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both local loans (including loans used within Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans used outside Hong Kong. Specifically, the total amount of local loans decreased slightly by 0.9% in the second half, while the total amount of loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%; in contrast, these figures had grown by 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the first six months. Figure 5.12 Loan Growth Analyzed by currency, HKD loans, after a 2.0% decline in the first half, remained broadly at the same level by the end of 2020 as at the end of June. Foreign currency loans, after a substantial increase of 10.6% in the first half of 2020, declined by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decrease in demand for USD loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand became slightly more optimistic compared to six months ago. The HKMA's "Credit Conditions Outlook Survey" in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decline during the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A). Due to the adverse impact of the pandemic on the repayment capacity of households and companies, the quality of bank loans deteriorated slightly but remained robust by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed in the second half of 2020. The total specific provision loan ratio of all authorized institutions moderated to 0.9% at the end of 2020 from 0.79% six months earlier, while the overdue and restructured loan ratio of all authorized institutions rose from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% by the end of 2020. For retail banks, the total specific provision loan ratio and the overdue and restructured loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Figure 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance weakened, yet inflationary pressures persisted and intensified across regions, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale outbreaks of the pandemic and the possibility that, if US inflation proves more persistent and widespread than expected, the tightening of monetary policy may exceed expectations. Should the Federal Reserve significantly tighten monetary policy, leading to a tightening of global financial conditions, this would place pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could significantly impact the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar depreciated slightly, but trading remained smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. On a full-year basis for 2021, the growth in total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the continued economic recovery. Coupled with the possibility that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected, these risk factors will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow down in late 2021, with weakness persisting into 2022, driven by increased restrictions on global mobility due to the spread of the highly contagious Omicron variant, alongside persistent supply bottlenecks that continue to pressure production. Meanwhile, amid supply-demand imbalances and labor shortages, global inflationary pressures have continued to intensify, spreading to a wide range of goods and services in major advanced economies, especially the United States. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has caused a sharp rise in commodity prices, which could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation. Increased volatility in financial markets may also lead to an undesirable tightening of global financial conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook remains subject to significant uncertainties. In the short term, should large-scale outbreaks occur, the reimposition of lockdown measures and a worsening of supply bottlenecks cannot be ruled out. In the United States, as the risk of inflation proving more persistent and widespread than expected grows, the Federal Reserve has adopted a more hawkish stance, accelerating its timeline for reducing asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussing balance sheet reduction. If the Federal Reserve needs to significantly tighten monetary policy, global financial conditions may also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt-servicing capacity and disorderly capital outflows that would place pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may expose global commodity prices to sustained upward pressure, exacerbate shortages in industrial supplies, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 will discuss whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds) can reduce liquidity risks for these funds during market stress, and examine the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, although the recovery momentum temporarily slowed in the third quarter as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed strict pandemic control measures. Meanwhile, regional economies focused on technology product exports (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from strong global demand for tech products. Although the market generally expects a broad recovery in emerging Asia in 2022, the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for economies with lower vaccination rates and constrained public health resources. Second, the Federal Reserve's accelerated policy normalization could trigger capital outflows from the region and intensify currency depreciation pressures; for regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support economic recovery, the trade-off between curbing capital outflows and supporting economic activity will become more difficult. Third, slowing growth in major economies, combined with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on trade growth prospects. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will transmit to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for monetary policy normalization by regional central banks will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and higher inflation sensitivity to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, to rebuild a sustainable and robust growth model, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines the sensitivity of stock returns to changes in climate risk and how this sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power rationing measures, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, due to the continued slump in the real estate market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure in the short term. Therefore, mainland authorities have prioritized stabilizing growth for this year and introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total value of onshore bond defaults in the second half of 2021, as well as defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) on onshore bonds, both decreased. Feature 3 discusses whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain controllable, as mainland banks (especially those with systemic importance) have limited exposure to developers, maintain low non-performing loan ratios, and hold high provision coverage ratios. The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, albeit at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real gross domestic product (GDP) grew moderately, supported by goods exports and private consumption benefiting from the continued global economic recovery, an improving local labor market, and the government's consumption voucher scheme. On a year-on-year basis, economic growth in the second half of 2021 was 5.1%, compared to 7.8% in the first half. For the full year of 2021, the economy grew by 6.4%, marking the first full year of positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local outbreaks and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures placed pressure on economic activity in Hong Kong. The government launched the fifth and sixth Anti-Epidemic and Fund Relief Funds, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guaranteed Personal Special Loan" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be optimized, with higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and longer repayment terms. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Interest-Only Payment" scheme until the end of October 2022. The scheme will also provide borrowers with a one-year option for partial principal repayment, which will also apply to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme." It is expected that the Hong Kong economy will continue to recover over the full year of 2022, but the growth pace will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and higher base effects. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. Government promotion of several major infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2022 to be between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are influenced by several uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalization. As the economy recovered, the labor market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by the end of the year. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labor market pressures re-emerged amid the new wave of local outbreaks. In addition, a decline in the number of online job advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local outbreaks and tightened pandemic control measures will place some pressure on the local labor market in the short term, particularly in industries involving face-to-face contact. In the longer term, labor market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures have increased moderately in recent months but remain contained. On a year-on-year basis, the core consumer price inflation rate rose slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualized core inflation rate, which reflects inflationary momentum, also rebounded in recent months, partly due to price increases for dining out and some energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term due to rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic. However, weak rental growth and moderate local labor cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the government projects overall inflation for 2022 at 2.1% and core inflation at 2.0%. Since September 2021, amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually weakened against the US dollar. Although the Hong Kong dollar experienced a slight rebound in October 2021, the upward momentum subsequently faded, primarily due to weak net southbound inflows via the Stock Connect and Shenzhen Stock Connect mechanisms, and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalizes monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained within the strong end of the currency peg range for most of the time, and trading continued smoothly and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from Hong Kong's banking system. Trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued smoothly and orderly. Due to ample interbank liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained low during the review period. The average mortgage interest rate for new loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore RMB banking business continued to thrive. In particular, Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to grow, with RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances reaching RMB 1,113.5 billion as of the end of January 2022. Although the outstanding balance of RMB loans decreased, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement System in 2021 rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from its efficient financial infrastructure, the north-south two-way mechanisms of the Stock Connect, Shenzhen Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of mainland China's capital account, increasing demand from international investors for RMB assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Greater Bay Area initiative. Stimulated by government monetary and fiscal policies, global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings drove major global stock markets higher overall in the last quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022. However, growing market concerns regarding the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid surging inflation risks, sharp rises in commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict have caused major global stock markets to consolidate since early January 2022.

Due to the rapid global spread of variant viruses (Delta and Omicron), coupled with persistent production bottlenecks, the global economy slowed significantly in the latter half of 2021, and growth momentum remained weak as 2022 began. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify, spreading to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted the Federal Reserve to shift its monetary policy stance toward hawkishness, exacerbating the risk that premature tightening of global financial conditions could pressure currently elevated asset valuations, while also adversely affecting emerging markets where the recovery remains generally lagging. Recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up energy and other commodity prices, triggering volatility in global financial markets and intensifying some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, the economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, with major technology product export economies in the region continuing to outperform other economies. Although the Omicron variant is not expected to severely impede the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty related to new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. Additionally, the normalization of Federal Reserve policy may trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, while slowing growth in major economies may drag down regional goods export growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on one hand, has led to rising commodity prices and increased inflation risks, and on the other, has weakened consumption and heightened global economic uncertainty, making the decision-making process for regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalization more complex. Economic growth in mainland China slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of novel coronavirus outbreaks, power rationing, and tightening measures in the real estate market. Looking ahead, the mainland economy may continue to face downward pressure from a cooling real estate market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In light of this, the government has prioritized stabilizing growth as its primary task for this year, with macroeconomic policies providing greater support. The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the fourth quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tightened restrictions on mobility worldwide. Furthermore, supply chain issues, such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production raw materials like semiconductors, continued to constrain production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasted in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support from the US and other major advanced economies, and slowing growth momentum in mainland China offsetting expected growth rebounds in other parts of Asia (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: IMF Real GDP Growth Forecasts. Amid slowing global economic growth, inflationary pressures also continued to increase during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, especially in the United States, which implemented substantial policy stimulus since the pandemic. Against a backdrop of supply bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labor shortages, inflationary pressures have spread to a wide range of goods and services (Figure 2.2). Moreover, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has driven up prices for various commodities, potentially exacerbating already elevated global inflationary pressures. Figure 2.2: Core Consumer Price Index Inflation Rates for Selected Economies. (1) Latest data for the US, UK, and Eurozone are for January 2022; others are for December 2021. (2) "Asian Advanced Economies" include Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Asian Emerging Market Economies" include mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties with substantial downside risks, which will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, and the policy responses of major central banks to inflation. Regarding the pandemic, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote work, and promoting vaccination. Compared to previous lockdown policies, these relatively relaxed measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, and preliminary signs of improvement in supply chain disruptions have emerged since the end of 2021 (Figure 2.3). However, in the event of large-scale outbreaks, the reimposition of lockdown measures cannot be ruled out, which could lead to a renewed deterioration of supply bottlenecks. Figure 2.3: Purchasing Managers' Index – Supplier Delivery Times Sub-index. If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually improve, providing some relief to commodity inflation. However, several developments may make the current high level of global inflation more persistent than expected, including the risk that the military conflict between Russia and Ukraine and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will drive up commodity prices; the lagged reflection of rising production costs in final selling prices; the potential for previously surging global residential property prices to drive up future rents; upward risks to wage growth due to labor market tightness; and rising inflation expectations. Particularly given that US inflation has recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at the December 2021 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, no longer characterizing high inflation as "transitory," and doubled the pace of asset purchase reductions from $150 billion to $300 billion per month, aiming to end the asset purchase program before March 2022 and initiating discussions on balance sheet reduction. In fact, recent market pricing indicates that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. In contrast, given the closer trade and financial ties between the Eurozone and Russia and Ukraine, the European Central Bank may face more significant policy trade-offs. In this context, coupled with persistently high global debt levels and asset valuations under prolonged accommodative policies, if sustained inflationary pressures force the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, it may expose borrowers to deteriorating solvency risks and trigger financial market volatility. Recently, with rising geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe, risk aversion in financial markets has increased, and signs of dollar shortages have emerged, including widening cross-currency basis swap spreads. Under conditions of premature tightening of global financial conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals and still affected by the pandemic may be vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Increased market volatility may also trigger redemption pressures on open-end funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature Article 1 discusses whether swing pricing (a liquidity management tool for open-end funds) can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during market stress and examines the potential limitations of this tool. In emerging Asia, the economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, but the spread of the Delta variant weakened growth momentum in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Figure 2.4). At the same time, as major technology product export hubs in the region, South Korea and Singapore continued to benefit from strong global demand for technology products, further widening the imbalance in regional recoveries. Additionally, inflationary pressures in several emerging Asian economies remain moderate. Figure 2.4: Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index. Markets generally expect a broad recovery in Asian emerging markets in 2022, but the region's short-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds: First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since the end of 2021, its economic impact remains less severe than previous infection waves; however, some regional economies with lagging vaccination rates and relatively tight public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, the normalization of Federal Reserve policy may trigger capital outflows and create depreciation pressure on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. On the long end of the yield curve, due to the historically high correlation between the two (Figure 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in long-term US yields could spill over to long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, intensifying the risk of adjustments in regional asset markets. Figure 2.5: Correlation between Asian 10-Year Sovereign Bond Yields and Corresponding US Treasury Yields. Third, the regional outlook for commodity trade faces uncertainties regarding slowing growth in major economies and a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, factors that may weaken regional export growth. Figure 2.6: US Imports from Emerging Asia and Real GDP. Fourth, although regional economies have relatively limited trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the rise in commodity prices triggered by the conflict will be transmitted to regional inflation while simultaneously weakening consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decision-making process for regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalization will become more complex. Central banks in some economies with weaker growth momentum and higher sensitivity of inflation to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. The pandemic also serves as a reminder for regional economies of the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models to prepare for other risks such as climate change. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature Article 2 investigates whether stock market returns are affected by changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance. The novel coronavirus pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turmoil, some open-end funds experienced significant outflows (Figure B1.1), placing pressure on their liquidity management. Figure B1.1: Fund Outflows from Selected Open-End Funds During the March 2020 Event. Besides investor liquidity needs, another reason for significant outflows may be that investors adopted a "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding potentially soaring redemption costs under market stress. To curb outflows driven by the first-mover advantage, some open-end funds adopted swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-end funds designed to reduce the first-mover advantage for investors. Although many open-end funds utilized swing pricing during this event, there is no empirical evidence indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-end funds. Against this backdrop, this feature article conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing could reduce fund outflows from open-end funds during the March 2020 event, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. Additionally, this article seeks to identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will propose policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming before other investors, thereby shifting redemption costs onto them. This advantage primarily exists in open-end funds using traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) incurred by investors are reflected in the open-end fund price after the transaction is executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem shares first do not bear these transaction costs. This becomes an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are anticipated. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced due to the expectation of rising redemption costs. This exacerbates the redemption pressure and liquidity risks faced by open-end funds.

Driven by continued growth in goods exports and private consumption, the Hong Kong economy resumed its recovery in the second half of 2021, achieving positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. As 2022 began, a new wave of local infections and the resulting tightening of social distancing measures placed pressure on local economic activity. The overall economy is projected to maintain its recovery throughout 2022, although the strength and pace of this recovery will be influenced by uncertainties and risks, including the pandemic and the normalization of US monetary policy. These adverse factors may also impact the outlook for the labour market, which had improved significantly in 2021. Although local inflation may rise slightly in the short term due to higher import prices, weak local rents and subdued labour costs are expected to contain overall price pressures.  The Hong Kong economy continued its recovery in the second half of 2021. On a year-on-year basis, real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by a further 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), albeit at a slower pace than in the first half of the year. For the full year of 2021, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first positive full-year growth since 2019. Figure 3.1 Growth Rate of Real GDP and Contributions of Major Expenditure Components On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity expanded moderately by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively (Figure 3.1). Domestically, an improving labour market, coupled with the government's consumption voucher scheme, boosted private consumption. However, overall investment expenditure moderated in the fourth quarter following two consecutive quarters of strong rebound. Externally, with the global economy continuing to recover, Hong Kong's goods trade remained robust, while services trade stayed weak, partly due to the stagnation of the visitor industry (Figure 3.2). On a net basis, external trade weighed on GDP in the third quarter but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter. Figure 3.2 Volume of Exports and Imports A new wave of local infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures placed pressure on Hong Kong's economic activity in early 2022. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-Epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the "100% Guarantee Personal Special Loan Scheme" and various guarantee products under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme" will be optimized, with higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and longer repayment terms. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, together with the banking sector, will also extend the "Pre-approved Interest-only Repayment" scheme to the end of October 2022. The scheme will also offer borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which will also apply to loans under the "SME Financing Guarantee Scheme". The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue its recovery throughout 2022, but the growth pace will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting a slowdown in global economic growth amid the ongoing pandemic and higher base effects. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. Government promotion of various civil engineering and infrastructure projects will also provide support to the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth for 2022 to be between 2.0% and 3.5%, while the average growth forecast from international organizations and private analysts stands at 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties and risks as outlined in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent developments in the pandemic, an accelerated pace of US monetary policy normalization, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the situation in Ukraine) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the global economy. On the other hand, if quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and mainland China resumes earlier than expected, it could stimulate local economic growth. With the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% by year-end (Figure 3.3). The total number of persons in employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent low in February 2021, although it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that pressure on the labour market re-emerged amid the new wave of local infections. Additionally, a decline in the number of online recruitment advertisements reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and tightened epidemic prevention measures are expected to exert some pressure on the local labour market in the short term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. In the longer run, the state of the labour market will depend on the development of the local pandemic and the pace of economic recovery. Figure 3.3 Labour Market Conditions Local inflationary pressures have increased somewhat in recent months but remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up slightly to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021, respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The underlying inflation rate measured on a three-month annualized basis, which reflects inflationary momentum, has also picked up in recent months. Specifically, prices for dining out and some energy-related items have accelerated, driven by the recovery in local demand and rising external prices (Figure 3.5). Meanwhile, the housing rent component of the Composite Consumer Price Index continued to decline broadly, thereby containing overall inflationary momentum (Figure 3.6). Although real unit labour costs remained subdued, they rose slightly in recent quarters, partly due to an improvement in real average salaries (Figure 3.7). Figure 3.4 Various Indicators Reflecting Consumer Price Inflation Figure 3.5 Hong Kong Import Prices Figure 3.6 Composite Consumer Price Index Rent Component and Market Rents Figure 3.7 Unit Labour Costs Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the short term due to rising import prices and logistics disruptions caused by the pandemic. However, weak rents and moderate local labour cost pressures should contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts overall inflation for 2022 to reach 2.4%, while the government forecasts overall inflation at 2.1% and underlying inflation at 2.0% for 2022.

Against the backdrop of risk-averse sentiment in the local equity market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate weakened during the review period. Given the ample liquidity in the HKD money market, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) remained at low levels. Overall, transactions in the HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong, with its ample foreign exchange reserves and robust banking system, is well-positioned to withstand the impact of such volatility. Overall, the HKD remained at the strong-side conversion band for most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the HKD/USD exchange rate has gradually weakened amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although improved market sentiment led to a slight rebound in the HKD in October 2021, the appreciation subsequently lost momentum, primarily due to weak net southbound inflows via the Stock Connect schemes (Chart 4.2) and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, initial public offering (IPO) fundraising activities continued to provide support for the HKD (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments data indicated that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no indications of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Chart 4.1: HKD Exchange Rate; Chart 4.2: Net Southbound Purchases via Stock Connect; Chart 4.3: Equity Funds Raised on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (HKEX). Although the US dollar strengthened during the review period, the HKD nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable due to the appreciation of the RMB against the HKD (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the HKD real effective exchange rate index broadly followed the trend of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4: Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the evolution of the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility. As US interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), an outflow of HKD liquidity (the speed and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions at the time) could lead to a weakening of the HKD and trigger the weak-side conversion guarantee. However, Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, enabling it to withstand capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the review period, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative. The HKD monetary base increased by 1.4% over the eight months since the end of June 2021, primarily driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness (CDIs). Reflecting the continued demand for Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) issued in response to banks' liabilities against the backdrop of ample liquidity in the banking system, EFBNs increased by HKD 119.7 billion to HKD 1.1887 trillion during the review period, while the total balances (before Discount Window operations) correspondingly decreased by HKD 119.9 billion to HKD 337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, the amount of currency notes and coins issued by the government remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5: Total Balances and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, total deposits of authorized institutions grew moderately by 4.5%, while HKD deposits increased slightly by 0.3%. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be subject to fluctuations due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs, as well as business and investment-related activities); therefore, it is appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For the full year of 2021, total deposits and HKD deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4%, respectively. Chart 4.6: Authorized Institution Deposits by Currency. Overall, transactions in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to proceed smoothly and in an orderly manner. Given the ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBOR remained at low levels despite market concerns over the tightening of US monetary policy (Chart 4.7). Partially reflecting market expectations of rising funding demands near year-end, HIBOR edged up slightly in December 2021. The average mortgage rate for new mortgages rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the prime lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide sufficient buffers in the event of large-scale capital market activities or volatility in financial markets. Chart 4.7: HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates. During the review period, the offshore RMB interbank market continued to operate normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demands near year-end, the overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced slight fluctuations in late December 2021, while the three-month offshore RMB HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8: Overnight and Three-Month Offshore RMB HIBOR Pricing. In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. Over the six months since the end of July 2021, the balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB 1.1135 trillion by the end of January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits increased by 33.5%, mainly driven by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in the balance of certificates of deposit. Chart 4.9: RMB Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong. Over the six-month period since July 2021, although the outstanding balance of RMB loans decreased by 10.2% to RMB 167.6 billion, RMB trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow. Between the end of July 2021 and the end of January 2022, local banks processed transactions totaling RMB 3.763 trillion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% compared to RMB 3.181 trillion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's substantial RMB liquidity pool continues to support a large volume of RMB payment and financing transactions. For the full year of 2021, the average daily turnover of the RMB Real-Time Gross Settlement (RMB RTGS) system increased from RMB 1.1915 trillion in 2020 to RMB 1.5226 trillion. Chart 4.10: RMB Trade Settlement Remittances. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit from the establishment of the northbound and southbound channels under Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening of the mainland's capital account, increased demand from international investors for RMB assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Greater Bay Area initiative. Major global stock markets continued to rise in the fourth quarter of 2021 but consolidated since January 2022 amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalation of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The Hong Kong stock market remained subdued in the fourth quarter of 2021, primarily weighed down by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Uncertainties regarding global risks and the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong led the Hang Seng Index to fall to a near two-year low by the end of February. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB bond market continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly influenced by a weakening sentiment in asset markets and a new wave of the local pandemic. Overall, major global stock markets continued to rise in the last quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to a record high of 3,262 points on January 4, 2022 (Chart 4.11). The global economic recovery and strong corporate earnings, supported by monetary and fiscal stimulus from governments, underpinned the rally in major global stock markets, although the pandemic remained the primary risk concern for investors throughout the year. However, major global stock markets have consolidated since early January 2022, amid growing concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amidst surging inflation risks, soaring commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In contrast, by the end of 2021, the Hong Kong stock market continued to underperform other major global stock markets. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at the end of 2021, a 14.1% decline from 2020. In early 2022, buying interest from value investors returned to the Hong Kong stock market, pushing the Hang Seng Index back to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties regarding the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index down to a near two-year low of 22,713 points by the end of February. Over the entire review period from the end of August 2021 to February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11: Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index. The implied volatility of the stock market fluctuated sharply at the end of November 2021 due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, before subsequently receding. Although the skew index retreated from its historical high in late June 2021, it remained at elevated levels, reflecting investor concerns that the long-term rebound in the stock market since the outbreak of the pandemic may face correction, and thus their willingness to allocate more capital to hedge against downside risks in the stock market (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12: Option Implied Volatility of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500, and Skew Index. Against the backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong stocks continued to record net inflows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, Southbound flows via Stock Connect recorded a significant net outflow in the third quarter of 2021, primarily due to concerns over the impact of regulatory changes in the mainland on technology stocks. However, buying activity via Southbound Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, with a cumulative net inflow of HKD 98.3 billion recorded by the end of February. During the review period, the cumulative net purchase amount increased by 5.7% to HKD 2.233 trillion (Chart 4.14). Chart 4.13: Net Capital Inflows to Hong Kong's Stock Market; Chart 4.14: Net Flows via Stock Connect. After recording a record high in funds raised in the first half of 2021, Hong Kong's primary market slowed down in the second half. In 2021, a total of 98 IPOs were listed, raising HKD 328.9 billion in aggregate (Chart 4.15), representing a 17.8% decline from the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth in the global public offering market, trailing only the Nasdaq, the New York Stock Exchange, and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15: Hong Kong Initial Public Offering Market. The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. Easing of mainland monetary policy and more Chinese concept stocks listing in Hong Kong as second listings in the primary market will improve sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market. However, the stock market still faces many adverse factors, including uncertainties regarding the evolution of the pandemic in Hong Kong, a faster-than-expected pace of normalization of US monetary policy, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The profitability of Hong Kong's retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The specific classification loan ratio rose slightly in the second half of 2021 but remained low by both historical and international standards. Underpinned by robust capital and liquidity positions, Hong Kong's banking sector remained resilient. During the review period, to further assist the economy in navigating difficult times, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to economic recovery. Coupled with the risk that the pace of US monetary policy normalization may be faster than expected, these factors will present challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. In the second half of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared to the same period in 2020. The weak profit performance was primarily driven by declines in net interest and non-interest income, alongside increased operating expenses. Consequently, the return on assets declined to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared to 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Figure 5.1). For the full year of 2021, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared to 2020, while the return on assets fell from 0.77% to 0.59%. Figure 5.1 reflects the ongoing impact of the low-interest-rate environment on retail bank profitability; the net interest margin of retail banks remained at a low level of 0.98% in the second half of 2021 (Figure 5.2). Figure 5.2 reflects year-end funding demand and the decline in the HKMA's overall surplus following the issuance of additional Exchange Fund Bills. As a result, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) recorded a slight increase in the fourth quarter of 2021. However, given the continued ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBOR remained at relatively low levels. Specifically, the three-month HIBOR rose slightly by 9 basis points from six months prior to 0.26% by the end of December 2021 (blue line in Figure 5.3). The cost of funds for retail banks remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite rate (an indicator measuring the average HKD cost of funds for retail banks) increased moderately by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months ago to 0.21% by the end of 2021 (green line in Figure 5.3). Figure 5.3 Interest Rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period averages for newly approved loans. Climate change impacts every aspect of life, and everyone has a responsibility to contribute to mitigating its effects. In this regard, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has devoted significant efforts to advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following the inclusion of our first Sustainability Report as a chapter in the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report last year, we have published the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time this year. I hope this report will enable readers to gain a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the resilience of Hong Kong's banking sector against climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our roles as a responsible investor and a sustainable development institution. Over the year, we have made significant progress in advancing sustainability across the HKMA's core functions. This report will detail our specific measures and initiatives, with key highlights as follows: Banks face climate risks in their daily operations. As the banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to enhance banks' capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we launched a two-year plan to integrate climate risk factors into our supervisory processes and to explore how technology can assist banks in assessing the impact of physical risks. Recognizing the increasing launch of green and sustainable products by banks, we have also shared best practices on managing these products effectively with the industry to strengthen banks' climate risk management capabilities. The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance development. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the "Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance" (Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy framework; this framework will enhance transparency in financial markets and promote greater consistency in green finance policies. Internationally, we are actively engaging with multiple international organizations to assist in formulating climate change policies and assessing their impact on financial stability. Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a particularly challenging year for global bond markets, Hong Kong's issuance of green and sustainable debt continued to record strong growth, increasing by 42% to a total of USD 80.5 billion, reaffirming Hong Kong's status as Asia's largest center for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². Relevant issuers include the Shenzhen Municipal Government and the Hainan Provincial Government, whose issuances once again demonstrate Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable capital between Mainland China and the international community. The robust development of Hong Kong's green bond market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Scheme. Since 2019, the HKMA has assisted the government in issuing green bonds totaling nearly USD 16 billion, with proceeds allocated to over 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and recycling, energy efficiency, and energy conservation. We have also assisted the government in achieving two "firsts": in May 2022, we facilitated the issuance of the first government green retail bonds totaling HKD 20 billion, which were the world's largest green retail bond issuance at the time; and in February 2023, we assisted in the issuance of the first tokenized green bonds. These were the world's first tokenized green bonds issued by a government, and this issuance also marked a milestone in successfully combining our strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and financial technology.
